Once the Sydney 2000 Olympic Band made their introduction, they took their place in front of the ceremony stage, and volunteers formed patterns to begin the Parade of Nations. Twenty eight of the larger nations entered under a music piece of their country played by the Marching Band (such as _[Aquarela do Brasil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aquarela\_do\_Brasil "Aquarela do Brasil")_ was played for [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Brazil at the 2000 Summer Olympics"), _[Land of Hope and Glory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land\_of\_Hope\_and\_Glory "Land of Hope and Glory")_ was played for [Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Great Britain at the 2000 Summer Olympics"), _[Sakura Sakura](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sakura\_Sakura "Sakura Sakura")_ was played for [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Japan at the 2000 Summer Olympics"), _[Siyahamba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siyahamba "Siyahamba")_ was played for [South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "South Africa at the 2000 Summer Olympics"), _[Born in the USA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born\_in\_the\_USA "Born in the USA")_/_[Stars and Stripes Forever](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stars\_and\_Stripes\_Forever "Stars and Stripes Forever")_ for the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "United States at the 2000 Summer Olympics"), _[Triumphal March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triumphal\_March "Triumphal March")_ from Verdi's [Aïda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A%C3%AFda "Aïda") for [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Italy at the 2000 Summer Olympics") and _[Down Under](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Down\_Under "Down Under")_ for [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Australia at the 2000 Summer Olympics")), while smaller countries entered in with various Olympic Anthems, Percussion Cadences, and _The Warriors_ as a nod to Australian wind band composer [Percy Grainger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percy_Grainger "Percy Grainger").[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWest200043-51) As is Olympic tradition, [Greece](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greece_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Greece at the 2000 Summer Olympics") entered first, and host nation Australia entered last.

As in the [last Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1996_Summer_Olympics "1996 Summer Olympics") in [Atlanta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlanta "Atlanta") and the [last Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics") in [Nagano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagano,_Nagano "Nagano, Nagano"), the countries entered in English alphabetical order. This was also to be seen during the [next Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics "2002 Winter Olympics"), in [Salt Lake City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_City "Salt Lake City").

A record of 199 nations entered the stadium with the exception of [Afghanistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Emirate_of_Afghanistan_(1996%E2%80%932001) "Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan (1996–2001)"), a nation banned by the [IOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") in 1999 because of the then government's oppression on women and its sports.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-52)[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-53) The parade of nations also featured a unified entrance by the athletes of both North and South Korea, holding a specially designed [Unification flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unification_flag "Unification flag").[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-54)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-:1-7) The two teams competed separately. Athletes from [East Timor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Timor "East Timor") marched directly in the opening ceremonies as _[Individual Olympic Athletes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Individual\_Olympic\_Athletes\_at\_the\_2000\_Summer\_Olympics "Individual Olympic Athletes at the 2000 Summer Olympics")_ and entered before the host nation. Without the existence of the National Olympic Committee, they were allowed to compete under the [Olympic flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_flag "Olympic flag").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-55)

### Dare To Dream

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Dare To Dream")]

Australian music legends, singers [John Farnham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Farnham "John Farnham") and [Olivia Newton-John](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olivia_Newton-John "Olivia Newton-John")[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-SevenNetworkMediaRelease-56) walked among the Olympic competitors and performed the theme song "_[Dare to Dream](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dare\_To\_Dream\_(Olympic\_Theme\_Song) "Dare To Dream (Olympic Theme Song)")_", which was written especially for the occasion by award-winning songwriters [Paul Begaud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Begaud "Paul Begaud"), Vanessa Corish and Wayne Tester. Begaud and Corish are songwriting collaborators both born and raised in Sydney.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-57)

### Opening Addresses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Opening Addresses")]

After a brief fanfare by [David Stanhope](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Stanhope?action=edit&redlink=1 "David Stanhope (page does not exist)"), the [President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Organising_Committee_for_the_Olympic_Games "President of the Organising Committee for the Olympic Games") of the [Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Organising_Committee_for_the_Olympic_Games "Sydney Organising Committee for the Olympic Games") (SOCOG), [Michael Knight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Knight_(Australian_politician) "Michael Knight (Australian politician)"), and the [President of the IOC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_International_Olympic_Committee "President of the International Olympic Committee"), [Juan Antonio Samaranch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Antonio_Samaranch "Juan Antonio Samaranch") made the opening addresses. In Knight's address, he spoke to the athletes directly about Australians love for sport, that while in the parade "the crowd cheered loudest for the home team, as it will at the sporting competitions," that "there is room in our hearts to support all of you wherever you have come from. Australians love sport, and we admire outstanding skill and courage."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-Olympicreview-openingceremony-58) Samaranch gave a recognition of Indigenous Australians, by summarising the artistic section in these words: "I would like to express our respect to those who have made Australia what it is today, a great country, with a special tribute to the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-:1-7)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-Olympicreview-openingceremony-58)

The event was officially opened by [Governor-General of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor-General_of_Australia "Governor-General of Australia")[Sir William Deane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Deane "William Deane"). This was the first occasion that a Summer Olympics in Commonwealth realm was not opened by the monarch or a member of the Royal Family, although it was the second overall, behind the [1988 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1988_Winter_Olympics "1988 Winter Olympics").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-59) Originally, SOCOG and the IOC gave the green light for the then Prime Minister [John Howard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Howard "John Howard"). However, in November 1999, he changed his mind and advised the IOC that the Governor-General should open the games. Howard said this was due to "a concern that my opening the Olympic Games would become a party political issue." This was a few days after the results of the [1999 Australian republic referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_Australian_republic_referendum "1999 Australian republic referendum") was known.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-60)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-61)

> "I declare open the Games of Sydney, celebrating the XXVII Olympiad of the modern era."

—HE The Hon Sir William Deane, AC KBE, Governor-General of the Commonwealth of Australia

### Olympic Flag

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Olympic Flag")]

Then 19-year-old pop star [Vanessa Amorosi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanessa_Amorosi "Vanessa Amorosi") sang "Heroes Live Forever" to signify the legacy left by sports stars all over the world.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-SevenNetworkMediaRelease-56)[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-CNNBrian-31) The song was composed by John Gillard and Trevor White.

During the song, an enormous white flag the size of the stadium field was passed over the audience on the southern stand and was brought down over the crowd by volunteers. Whilst this happened, images of past sports legends were displayed on the flag. When the flag reached the athletes, a [Dove of Peace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games_ceremony#Doves "Olympic Games ceremony") was projected, followed by the Olympic Rings.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-CNNBrian-31) This section was a partial recreation of a segment from the [1992 Summer Olympics opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1992_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony "1992 Summer Olympics opening ceremony"), where a large Olympic flag covered the athletes.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-FOOTNOTEWest200051-62)

The official [Olympic Flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Flag "Olympic Flag") was then carried around the arena by eight former Australian Olympic champions: [Bill Roycroft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Roycroft "Bill Roycroft"), [Murray Rose](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murray_Rose "Murray Rose"), [Liane Tooth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liane_Tooth "Liane Tooth"), [Gillian Rolton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gillian_Rolton "Gillian Rolton"), [Marjorie Jackson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marjorie_Jackson "Marjorie Jackson"), [Lorraine Crapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorraine_Crapp "Lorraine Crapp"), [Michael Wenden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Wenden "Michael Wenden") and [Nick Green](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Green_(rower) "Nick Green (rower)"). It was then handed over to eight [Australia's Federation Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia's_Federation_Guard "Australia's Federation Guard") members, who carried and raised the flag. During the raising of the Olympic flag, the [Olympic Hymn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Hymn "Olympic Hymn") was sung in Greek by the Millennium Choir of the [Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_Orthodox_Archdiocese_of_Australia "Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia"), representing Australia's large Greek population.

The Olympic Oaths were taken on behalf of the athletes by then captain of the Australian Women's Hockey Team [Rechelle Hawkes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rechelle_Hawkes "Rechelle Hawkes"),[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-63) and on behalf of the officials by Australian Water Polo Referee [Peter Kerr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peter_Kerr_(water_polo) "Peter Kerr (water polo)").[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-64)

For the first time in recent Olympic history, the opening ceremony concluded with the lighting of the [Olympic cauldron](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_flame "Olympic flame"). [Tina Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tina_Arena "Tina Arena"), the [Sydney Children's Choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Children's_Choir "Sydney Children's Choir") and the [Melbourne Symphony Orchestra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Symphony_Orchestra "Melbourne Symphony Orchestra") performed _The Flame_,[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-SevenNetworkMediaRelease-56) while showing footage of some highlights of the [torch relay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay "2000 Summer Olympics torch relay") on the large screens, then cutting to live footage outside the stadium of Australian Olympic Gold Medalist [Herb Elliott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herb_Elliott "Herb Elliott") with the torch.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-65)

Then, celebrating [100 years of women's participation in the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Participation_of_women_in_the_Olympics "Participation of women in the Olympics"),[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-SMH-Stephens-16) all of the last torch bearers were women and Olympic Medalists: [Betty Cuthbert](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Betty_Cuthbert "Betty Cuthbert") and [Raelene Boyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raelene_Boyle "Raelene Boyle"),[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-CNNBrian-31)[Dawn Fraser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawn_Fraser "Dawn Fraser"),[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-abc-TraceyHolmes-66)[Shirley Strickland de la Hunty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirley_Strickland_de_la_Hunty "Shirley Strickland de la Hunty"),[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-abc-TraceyHolmes-66)[Shane Gould](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shane_Gould "Shane Gould")[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-CNNBrian-31) and [Debbie Flintoff-King](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Debbie_Flintoff-King "Debbie Flintoff-King")[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-abc-TraceyHolmes-66) was the last torchbearer inside the stadium track, before handing it over to [Cathy Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathy_Freeman "Cathy Freeman").[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-Guardianlb_flame-67) Freeman then climbed a long set of stairs towards a circular pool of water. She walked into the middle of the water and ignited the cauldron around her feet in a ring of fire. The cauldron then rose out from the water, above Freeman's head, and then was transported up a long waterfall, where it finally rested on a tall silver pedestal above the stadium as the ceremony concluded with a fireworks display.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-:1-7)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-SMH-Stephens-16) The final section of torchbearers and the lighting of the cauldron was accompanied by [Te Deum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_Deum_(Berlioz) "Te Deum (Berlioz)") by French composer [Hector Berlioz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hector_Berlioz "Hector Berlioz"), performed by the Sydney Symphony Orchestra, the [Sydney Philharmonia Choir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Philharmonia_Choirs "Sydney Philharmonia Choirs"), and the Sing 2001 children's choir.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-68)

The planned climax to the ceremony was delayed by a technical glitch of a malfunctioned limit switch, which also severed the communications cable to override the program.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-CXNetworkCauldron-69) This meant that the Olympic flame was suspended in mid-air for about four minutes, rather than immediately rising up the waterfall to the top of the stadium. In interviews after the ceremony, the organizers stated that when the cause of the problem was discovered, engineers overrode the program and the cauldron continued its course.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-:2-8)[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-CXNetworkCauldron-69) 20 years later, some engineers stated it was fixed through a backup radio signal to the cauldron.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-MySydney2000-cauldron-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-ABCNews-Knight-71) Moreover, the gas bottles for the cauldron were close to empty before it was attached to a main gas line, and the backup flames were missing.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-CXNetworkCauldron-69)

*   Concept: Ric Birch, Michael Scott-Mitchell
*   Segment Director: [Richard Wherrett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Wherrett "Richard Wherrett")
*   Cauldron Designer: Michael Scott-Mitchell

## Reviews

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Reviews")]

The ceremony was given rave reviews by the local media. IOC President Juan Antonio Samaranch thought it was a successful opening ceremony, giving it a 10-out-of-10 score.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-72)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-IrishTimes-73) Then [Premier of New South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_New_South_Wales "Premier of New South Wales")[Bob Carr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bob_Carr "Bob Carr") claimed a few days after the ceremony that it was perhaps the most important work of art ever produced in Australia's history.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBirch2004304-74)[The Sydney Morning Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Sydney_Morning_Herald "The Sydney Morning Herald") said, "It was daring. It was dignified. It was witty. It was breathtaking in its large-scale theatricality."[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-heraldreview-75) Journalist Peter FitzSimons said that the atmosphere at the stadium that night was electric and said of the Artistic section that "it was a colourful and colossal kaleidoscope on overdrive, with Australia's cultural buttons being played like piano keys in the hands of a master."[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-Fitzsimons-32)_[The Sunday Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Daily\_Telegraph\_(Sydney) "The Daily Telegraph (Sydney)")_ described it as a "truly great moment" in Australian history, going on to say that about the Awakening segment that it was "Australia's global declaration that it acknowledged its indigenous people and cared about their future, while feeling considerable regret – yes even sorrow – about the past." John Lombard from [ABC News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ABC_News_(Australia) "ABC News (Australia)") pointed out that having Cathy Freeman be the athlete to light the cauldron was a coup, as the extra symbolism of many white, Australian-born women passing the torch to an Aboriginal athlete "hit all the right buttons".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-IrishTimes-73)

Foreign press reaction was also very positive; _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ also noted the themes of reconciliation given the political climate.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-:1-7) The London _[Daily Express](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Express "Daily Express")_'s Shekhar Bhatia described Webster as "the toast of the town and a global sensation".[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-SH-Internationalreviews-76) London's _[Daily Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Telegraph "Daily Telegraph")_ wrote that the "four-hour spectacle must be classified an unqualified success."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-SH-Internationalreviews-76) The only negative review reported at the time was from _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Washington\_Post "The Washington Post")_, where [Sally Jenkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sally_Jenkins "Sally Jenkins") described the ceremony as traditional, expensive and too long; as something that "a roving band of wild dogs couldn't cure."[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-SH-Internationalreviews-76) She did, however, go on to say that the lighting of the cauldron was "almost worth the price of admission" due to its symbolism of the nation's reconciliation.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-WP-Jenkins-77)

## Legacy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony&action=edit&section=21 "Edit section: Legacy")]

A major theme in this ceremony was of reconciliation between Australia and the Australian Indigenous past. In the years leading up to the Olympics, Indigenous reconciliation was becoming a central social and political issue after the release of the [Bringing Them Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bringing_Them_Home "Bringing Them Home") report.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-:1-7) In the ceremony's Media Guide, the author notes that four months earlier, during the [Corroboree 2000 reconciliation event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconciliation_in_Australia#Corroboree_2000 "Reconciliation in Australia"), 250,000 Australians of all backgrounds walked across Sydney Harbour Bridge as support for recognition of past wrongs towards the First Nations peoples.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-corroboree2000-78) The Awakening segment was seen as a key critical segment to the ceremony by showing Indigenous dance and music in its own context for over 11 minutes and in a deep and significant way. Birch anecdotally pointed out that in the years after the ceremony there was an increase of [Indigenous Australian Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_studies#Indigenous_Australian_studies "Australian studies") in NSW Public Schools curriculum.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-FOOTNOTEBirch2004303-79) In later sporting events in Australia, similar segments were developed for the [2006 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_Commonwealth_Games_opening_ceremony "2006 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony"), and the [2018 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Commonwealth_Games_opening_ceremony "2018 Commonwealth Games opening ceremony") started with a vision of Australian history from the point of view of the original people of the state of Queensland.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-TheConversation-80)

In November 2000, the television footage of Cathy Freeman lighting the cauldron was declared "the sporting image of the year" and won a "Golden Podum" by Sportel, a major international sports television convention held annually in Monaco.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-81) At the [first Helpmann Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1st_Helpmann_Awards "1st Helpmann Awards") the ceremony was awarded Best Special Event/Performance, Best Sound Design, and Best Costume Design for the Deep Sea Dreaming segment, and Best Scenic Design for the Awakening segment.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-82)

The Arts Unit of NSW Education played an important role in providing primary and high school children across NSW to perform at Olympic events. The Sydney 2000 Olympic Band continues as a secondary public school ensemble in New South Wales. Now named the NSW Public Schools Millennium Marching Band, the band performs at large-scale and televised events in both Australia and overseas. The smaller ensemble (consisting of around 100 members) traveled to Beijing for the [2001 Summer Universiade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_Summer_Universiade "2001 Summer Universiade") and [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") and performed in the United States in 2015 in San Francisco, Seattle and Los Angeles.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-83)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-NSWEducat-84) The Sing 2001 choir continued to perform after the Olympics during major events in 2001 celebrating the Centenary of Australian Federation.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_opening_ceremony#cite_note-85)

The **2002 Winter Olympics**, officially the **XIX Olympic Winter Games** and commonly known as **Salt Lake 2002** ([Arapaho](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arapaho_language "Arapaho language"): _Niico'ooowu' 2002_; [Gosiute Shoshoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosiute_dialect "Gosiute dialect"): _Tit'-so-pi 2002_; [Navajo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navajo_language "Navajo language"): _Sooléí 2002_; [Shoshoni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shoshoni_language "Shoshoni language"): _Soónkahni 2002_), were an international winter [multi-sport event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-sport_event "Multi-sport event") that was held from February 8 to 24, 2002, in and around [Salt Lake City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_City "Salt Lake City"), Utah, United States.

Salt Lake City was selected as the host city in June 1995 at the 104th [IOC Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOC_Session "IOC Session"). They were the eighth Olympics to be hosted by the United States, and the most recent to be held in the country until 2028, when Los Angeles hosts the [Games of the XXXIV Olympiad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_Summer_Olympics "2028 Summer Olympics"). The 2002 Winter Olympics and [Paralympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Paralympic_Winter_Games "2002 Paralympic Winter Games") were both organized by the [Salt Lake Organizing Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_Organizing_Committee_for_the_Olympic_and_Paralympic_Winter_Games_of_2002 "Salt Lake Organizing Committee for the Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games of 2002") (SLOC), the first time that both events were organized by a single committee, and inspiring other Olympic and Paralympic Games to be organized by such since then.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-SLOC_Official_Report_p35-2) These were the first Olympic Games under the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) [presidency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_International_Olympic_Committee "President of the International Olympic Committee") of [Jacques Rogge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Rogge "Jacques Rogge").

The Games featured 2,399 athletes from 78 nations, participating in 78 events in 15 disciplines. Norway topped the medal table, with 13 gold and 25 medals overall, while Germany finished with the most total medals, winning 36 (with 12 of them gold). The hosting United States was third by gold medals and second by overall medals, with 10 and 34 respectively. Australia notably became the first [Southern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere "Southern Hemisphere") country to ever win gold medals at the Winter Olympics.

The Games finished with a budgetary surplus of US$40 million; the surplus was used to fund the formation of the Utah Athletic Foundation—which has continued to maintain the facilities built for these Olympics. The venues have continued to be used for national and international winter sports events after the Olympics, leading to the Winter Olympics return to Salt Lake City for the [2034 games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2034_Winter_Olympics "2034 Winter Olympics"), 32 years after the city played host in 2002.

## Host city selection

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Host city selection")]

Main article: [Bids for the 2002 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bids_for_the_2002_Winter_Olympics "Bids for the 2002 Winter Olympics")

Salt Lake City was chosen over Québec City, Canada; Sion, Switzerland; and Östersund, Sweden, on June 16, 1995, at the 104th [IOC Session](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IOC_Session "IOC Session") in [Budapest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Budapest "Budapest"), Hungary.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-3) Salt Lake City had previously come in second during the bids for the [1998 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics"), awarded to [Nagano](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nagano,_Nagano "Nagano, Nagano"), Japan, and had offered to be the provisional host of the [1976 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Winter_Olympics "1976 Winter Olympics") when the original host, [Denver, Colorado](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denver,_Colorado "Denver, Colorado"), withdrew. The 1976 Winter Olympics were ultimately awarded to [Innsbruck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innsbruck "Innsbruck"), Austria.

There was a [scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympic_bid_scandal "2002 Winter Olympic bid scandal") involving allegations of bribery used to win the rights to the Games. Prior to its successful bid, Salt Lake City had attempted four times to secure the games, failing each time. In 1998, members of the [International Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Olympic_Committee "International Olympic Committee") (IOC) were accused of taking gifts from the [Salt Lake Organizing Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_Organizing_Committee_for_the_Olympic_and_Paralympic_Winter_Games_of_2002 "Salt Lake Organizing Committee for the Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games of 2002") (SLOC) during the bidding process. The allegations resulted in the expulsion of several IOC members and the adoption of new IOC rules. Although nothing strictly illegal had been done, it was felt that the acceptance of the gifts was morally dubious. In addition, legal charges were brought against the leaders of Salt Lake's bid committee by the [United States Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-NY_Times_dec2003-4) Investigations were also launched into prior bidding process by other cities, finding that members of the IOC received bribes during the bidding process for both the [1998 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1998_Winter_Olympics "1998 Winter Olympics") and [2000 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-5) In response to the scandal, [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney") was hired as the new president and CEO of the Salt Lake Organizing Committee in February 1999.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-:0-6)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-7)

### Budget

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Budget")]

In February 1999, in response to the [bid scandal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympic_bid_scandal "2002 Winter Olympic bid scandal") and a financial shortfall for the Games, [Mitt Romney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney "Mitt Romney"), then CEO of the private equity firm [Bain Capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bain_Capital "Bain Capital") (and future [U.S. presidential candidate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_United_States_presidential_election "2012 United States presidential election"), [U.S. Senator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Senator "U.S. Senator"), and [Governor of Massachusetts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Governor_of_Massachusetts "Governor of Massachusetts")), was [hired](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitt_Romney#2002_Winter_Olympics "Mitt Romney") as the new president and CEO of the [Salt Lake Organizing Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salt_Lake_Organizing_Committee_for_the_Olympic_and_Paralympic_Winter_Games_of_2002 "Salt Lake Organizing Committee for the Olympic and Paralympic Winter Games of 2002").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-:0-6) Romney, Kem C. Gardner, a Utah commercial real estate developer, and Don Stirling, the Olympics' local marketing chief, raised "millions of dollars from Mormon families with pioneer roots: the Eccles family, whose forebears were important industrialists and bankers" to help rescue the Games, according to a later report.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-9) An additional [US$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_dollar "United States dollar")410 million was received from the federal government.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-10) U.S. federal subsidies amounted to $1.3 billion (for infrastructure improvements only), compared to $45 billion of federal funding received by the organizing committee of the [2014 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Winter_Olympics "2014 Winter Olympics") from the Russian government.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-The_Guardian-11)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-GAO-12) The Games were financially successful, raising more money with fewer sponsors than any prior Olympic Games, which left SLOC with a surplus of [$](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USD "USD")40 million. The surplus was used to create the Utah Athletic Foundation, which maintains and operates many of the remaining Olympic venues.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-Marketing_Matters_6_2002-13)

_The Oxford Olympics Study_ established the outturn cost of the Salt Lake City 2002 Winter Olympics at US$2.5 billion in 2015-dollars and cost overrun at 24% in real terms.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-14) This includes sports-related costs only, that is, (i) _operational costs_ incurred by the organizing committee to stage the Games, e.g., expenditures for technology, transportation, workforce, administration, security, catering, ceremonies, and medical services, and (ii) _direct capital costs_ incurred by the host city and country or private investors to build, e.g., the competition venues, the Olympic village, international broadcast center, and media and press center, which are required to host the Games. Indirect capital costs are _not_ included, such as for road, rail, or airport infrastructure, or for hotel upgrades or other business investment incurred in preparation for the Games but not directly related to staging the Games. The cost and cost overrun for Salt Lake City 2002 compares with costs of US$2.5 billion and a cost overrun of 13% for Vancouver 2010, and costs of US$51 billion[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-The_Guardian-11) and a cost overrun of 289% for Sochi 2014, the latter being the most costly Olympics to date. The average cost for Winter Games since 1960 is US$3.1 billion, average cost overrun is 142%.

### Security

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Security")]

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d7/WinterOlympicsMP2002.png/250px-WinterOlympicsMP2002.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:WinterOlympicsMP2002.png)

Spc. Patrick Jean-Mary, of Warwick, R.I., inspects two forms of identification during the 2002 Winter Olympic Games in Salt Lake City

The 2002 Winter Games were the first Olympic Games to take place since the [September 11 attacks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks "September 11 attacks"), which meant a higher level of security than ever before provided for the games. As a result, the [Office of Homeland Security](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Homeland_Security "Office of Homeland Security") (OHS) designated the Olympics a [National Special Security Event](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Special_Security_Event "National Special Security Event") (NSSE). Aerial surveillance and radar control was provided by the [U.S. Marines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Marine_Corps "U.S. Marine Corps") of Marine Air Control Squadron 2, Detachment C, from [Cherry Point, North Carolina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cherry_Point,_North_Carolina "Cherry Point, North Carolina"). The [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") and NSA arranged with [Qwest Communications](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qwest "Qwest") to use intercept equipment for a period of less than six months around the time of the 2002 Winter Olympics.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-15)

### Transportation

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Transportation")]

The largest [public transport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_transport "Public transport") project completed for the Games was the [TRAX light rail system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TRAX_(light_rail) "TRAX (light rail)"), which first began operations ahead of the Games in 1999.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-16)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-2linesopen-17)

To help reduce vehicle traffic to Soldier Hollow, and to provide a tourist attraction for attendees, [Heber Valley Railroad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heber_Valley_Railroad "Heber Valley Railroad") offered service to [Wasatch Mountain State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasatch_Mountain_State_Park "Wasatch Mountain State Park") on [steam locomotives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steam_locomotives "Steam locomotives") during the Games. After arriving, passengers then embarked to Soldier Hollow on horse-drawn [sleighs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sled "Sled").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-auto-18)[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-19)

### Venues

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Venues")]

Main article: [Venues of the 2002 Winter Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venues_of_the_2002_Winter_Olympics "Venues of the 2002 Winter Olympics")

[![Image 12](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/Slcolympics.jpg/250px-Slcolympics.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Slcolympics.jpg)

Salt Lake City during the 2002 Winter Olympics

Work on venues for the 2002 Winter Olympics began as early as 1989, following the passing of a state referendum that authorized the use of taxpayer money to publicly fund the construction of new facilities for a Winter Olympics bid in 1998 or 2002. Their construction was overseen by the Salt Lake Olympic Bid Committee and the Utah Sports Authority—a body created under the referendum.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-21)

New facilities built for the Games included the [Utah Olympic Oval](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_Olympic_Oval "Utah Olympic Oval") in [Kearns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kearns,_Utah "Kearns, Utah"), [Utah Olympic Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utah_Olympic_Park "Utah Olympic Park") in [Summit County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summit_County,_Utah "Summit County, Utah"), [The Ice Sheet at Ogden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Ice_Sheet_at_Ogden "The Ice Sheet at Ogden"), and [Soldier Hollow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soldier_Hollow "Soldier Hollow") at the [Wasatch Mountain State Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wasatch_Mountain_State_Park "Wasatch Mountain State Park")—the furthest competition venue from Salt Lake City.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-auto-18) The [E Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/E_Center "E Center") in [West Valley City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Valley_City,_Utah "West Valley City, Utah")[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-22) and the [Peaks Ice Arena](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peaks_Ice_Arena "Peaks Ice Arena") in [Provo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provo,_Utah "Provo, Utah") were also built with support from the SLOC, and co-hosted hockey.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-24)

[Delta Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Center "Delta Center") hosted figure skating and short track speed skating; it was renamed _Salt Lake Ice Center_ for the duration of the Games due to IOC sponsorship rules.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-:02-25)[Rice-Eccles Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rice-Eccles_Stadium "Rice-Eccles Stadium") at the [University of Utah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Utah "University of Utah") hosted the opening and closing ceremonies.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-:1-26) The [Olympic Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Village "Olympic Village") was built at historic [Fort Douglas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fort_Douglas "Fort Douglas"), whose land had been acquired by the University of Utah to construct new residences. The SLOC provided funding to the project in exchange for its use during the Olympics.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-27)

Main Street in [Park City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Park_City,_Utah "Park City, Utah") was converted into a pedestrian plaza during the Games, with festivities such as concerts, firework shows, and sponsor presences.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-29) Medal presentations took place in downtown Salt Lake City; the stage for the ceremony featured the [Hoberman Arch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hoberman_Arch "Hoberman Arch"), an arch-shaped metal "curtain" designed by [Chuck Hoberman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Hoberman "Chuck Hoberman").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-SLT_unveiling-30)

The 2002 Cultural Olympiad, which ran from January to March 2002,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-prog-41) was an arts festival that accompanied the 2002 Winter Olympics. It included specially commissioned works, such as [Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alvin_Ailey_American_Dance_Theater "Alvin Ailey American Dance Theater")'s work _Here...Now_ inspired by the life of Olympian [Florence Griffith Joyner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Florence_Griffith_Joyner "Florence Griffith Joyner"), accompanied by music by [Wynton Marsalis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wynton_Marsalis "Wynton Marsalis").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-42) An art exhibition was held at [Springville Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Springville_Museum_of_Art "Springville Museum of Art") that celebrated 150 years of Utah's art history.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-43) The programme also featured many other performances, including dance, theatre, singing, and literature, as well as the glass art of [Dale Chihuly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dale_Chihuly "Dale Chihuly").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-prog-41)

### Olympic Music

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Olympic Music")]

Call of the Champions is a cantata-fanfare for orchestra and choir composed by [John Williams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Williams "John Williams") for the 2002 Winter Olympics.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-Filmtracks-44) Premiering at the Opening Ceremony on February 8, 2002, it began with the call by the [Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tabernacle_Choir_at_Temple_Square "Tabernacle Choir at Temple Square") of "Citius! Altius! Fortius!" (Faster, Higher, Stronger), which is the Olympic Motto chosen by the founder of the modern Games, Baron [Pierre de Coubertin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_de_Coubertin "Pierre de Coubertin"). Williams added another Latin word as well: "Clarius," meaning "clearer."

### Torch relay

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Torch relay")]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/57/Olympic_torch.jpg/250px-Olympic_torch.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Olympic_torch.jpg)

Torchbearer in Olympic [livery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livery "Livery")

Main article: [2002 Winter Olympics torch relay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics_torch_relay "2002 Winter Olympics torch relay")

The torch relay ceremonially began on November 19, 2001, with the traditional kindling of an Olympic flame in Olympia, Greece.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-45) On December 3, Greek skier Thanassis Tsailas lit the first torch from the cauldron, and transferred its flame to a ceremonial lantern for transport to Atlanta, where it arrived on December 4 to officially launch the U.S. leg of the relay.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-KSL_torch_relay-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-KSL_arrival-47) The route of the relay covered 13,500 miles (21,700 km), passed through 300 communities and 46 U.S. states, and was carried by 12,012 torchbearers.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-SLOC_Official_Report_route_plan-48)

The torch was modeled after an icicle, with a slight curve to represent speed and fluidity. The torch measures 33 inches (84 cm) long, 3 inches (7.6 cm) wide at the top, 0.5 inches (1.3 cm) at the bottom, and was designed by Axiom Design of Salt Lake City.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-SLOC_torch_info-49)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-50) It was created with three sections, each with its own meaning and representation.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-SLOC_torch_info-49)

## Marketing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=10 "Edit section: Marketing")]

### Branding & Emblem

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Branding & Emblem")]

The overall branding of the 2002 Winter Olympics, the "Look of the Games" design was named "Land of Contrast — Fire and Ice", which featured a palette of warm and cool colors to contrast the warmer, rugged, [red-rock areas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colorado_Plateau "Colorado Plateau") of Southern Utah from the colder, mountainous regions of Northern Utah.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-SLOC_Official_Report_designs-51) The three main color palettes were: _Amber Gold_, _Sunset Orange_ and _Mountain Shadow Blue_: With accented hue variations of the palette.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-52)

*   _sandstone_
*   _amber_*   _wildfire_
*   _redrock_*   _azure lapis_
*   _decorative blue_*   _dark turquoise_
*   _lake_

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/Boeing_777-200.jpg/250px-Boeing_777-200.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Boeing_777-200.jpg)

[Delta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delta_Air_Lines "Delta Air Lines")'s [Boeing 777](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing_777 "Boeing 777")-200ER (N864DA) in [livery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Livery "Livery") commemorating the Games

The emblem was named "Crystal Rhythm". It featured a six pointed [snow crystal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowflake "Snowflake"), again with the three main colors representing Utahs southern deserts and its high snowy mountain ranges. Designed to resemble an Olympic cauldron, a flame, as well as a sun rising from behind mountains. The orange center section of the flame was intended to reflect traditional [Navajo weaving](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navajo_weaving "Navajo weaving").[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-SLOC_Official_Report_designs-51) The emblem logo was designed by [Landor Associates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landor_Associates "Landor Associates") and unveiled in August 1997.

The official event pictograms were inspired by [branding irons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Branding_irons "Branding irons"), and the line thickness and 30-degree angles mirrored those of the emblem.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-SLOC_Official_Report_designs-51)

### Mascots

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Mascots")]

Main article: [Powder, Copper and Coal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder,_Copper_and_Coal "Powder, Copper and Coal")

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/3/39/Salt_Lake_2002_Olympic_Mascots.svg/250px-Salt_Lake_2002_Olympic_Mascots.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Salt_Lake_2002_Olympic_Mascots.svg)

[Powder, Copper and Coal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powder,_Copper,_Coal_and_Otto "Powder, Copper, Coal and Otto"), the 2002 Olympic mascots

The designs of the mascots of the 2002 Winter Olympics were unveiled on May 19, 1999, during an event marking 1,000 days until the opening ceremony.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-53) The mascots represent three animals native to the [western United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_United_States "Western United States") — a [snowshoe hare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowshoe_hare "Snowshoe hare"), [coyote](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coyote "Coyote"), and [American black bear](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_black_bear "American black bear") respectively, with each mascot symbolizing a character from the legends of local Native Americans, and wearing a charm around their neck with an original [Anasazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancestral_Puebloans "Ancestral Puebloans") or [Fremont](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fremont_culture "Fremont culture")-style [petroglyph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroglyph "Petroglyph"). For the first time in Olympic history, the names of the mascots were determined by a public vote, using name suggestions submitted by local students; on September 25, the names of the mascots were officially announced as Powder, Copper, and Coal respectively.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-DN_names_announced-54)

## Participating National Olympic Committees

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2002_Winter_Olympics&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Participating National Olympic Committees")]

A total of 78 teams qualified at least one athlete to compete in the Games. Five NOCs made their Winter Olympic debut in Salt Lake, including Cameroon, Hong Kong, Nepal, Tajikistan, and Thailand.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_Winter_Olympics#cite_note-Nations-55) Costa Rica and Lebanon returned to the Winter games after a 10-year absence, and Fiji, Mexico and San Marino returned after 8 years. Four countries, Luxembourg, North Korea, Portugal and Uruguay which were at the 1998 Games, did not participate in 2002.

The **2000 Summer Olympics torch relay** was the transferral of the [Olympic Flame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Flame "Olympic Flame") to [Sydney](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney "Sydney"), [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia"), that built up to the [2000 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics "2000 Summer Olympics"). The torch travelled to various island nations as part of a tour of [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania "Oceania") before beginning an extensive journey around Australia. For the first time the Flame was taken underwater, with a special flare-like torch taken on a dive down to the [Great Barrier Reef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Barrier_Reef "Great Barrier Reef"). At the opening ceremony the cauldron was lit by [Aboriginal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_Australians "Indigenous Australians") athlete [Cathy Freeman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cathy_Freeman "Cathy Freeman").

## Torch

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Torch")]

The design of the torch reflected three famed areas of Australian culture: the [boomerang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boomerang "Boomerang"), the [Sydney Opera House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Opera_House "Sydney Opera House"), and the waters of the [Pacific Ocean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacific_Ocean "Pacific Ocean"). The concept also reflected the elements of earth, fire, and water.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-OfficialReport-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-eweek-2) This was achieved across three layers of the torch. The first, inner layer contains the fuel system and combustor, the second contains the fuel canister, and the outer layer is a specially textured aluminium shell. A combination of copper, brass, aluminium, and stainless steel was used in its construction, and the fuel comprised 65 percent butane and 35 percent propane. In total, 14,000 torches were produced.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-eweek-2) The distance covered by each torchbearer was 105.478 km.

## Torchbearers

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Torchbearers")]

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/6e/Torch_bearer.jpg/250px-Torch_bearer.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Torch_bearer.jpg)

Fred Atkins taking the Torch through [Taree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taree "Taree"), New South Wales

A total of 13,400 torch-bearers were involved in the relay. The Greek leg of the route saw 800 people carry the torch, while 1,500 people were involved across [Oceania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oceania "Oceania"). As part of the vast traversal of Australia, 11,000 people carried the torch within the country.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-3)[Anna Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Booth "Anna Booth") was the Australian who chaired the 2000 Summer Olympics torch relay committee and she brought the torch to Australian soil on 8 June.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-4)

The first Australian torch-bearer was Sophie Gosper in May, the daughter of International Olympic Committee (IOC) Vice-President [Kevan Gosper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kevan_Gosper "Kevan Gosper"). Her selection caused considerable controversy with accusations of corruption directed at the [Hellenic Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenic_Olympic_Committee "Hellenic Olympic Committee") (HOC). Greek-Australian Yianna Souleles was originally due to receive the torch in Olympia but she was replaced at late notice by Gosper. Kevan Gosper accepted the invitation for his daughter to carry the torch while claiming to be unaware that this would make her the first Australian to have the honour.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-ISOR-5)

The HOC's invitation was seen as an attempt to carry favour with the IOC after being warned that its delays put the planned 2004 Olympics (scheduled to be held in Greece) in jeopardy.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-6) Gosper's acceptance of the invitation was portrayed by the media as being [nepotistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nepotism "Nepotism") and inappropriate, with Australian politicians, Olympic athletes, and officials from various Olympic Committees condemning the move. Gosper initially defended his actions but would go on to make a public apology, claiming that fatherly pride had clouded his judgement. He gave up his role in the relay at the [Melbourne Cricket Ground](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melbourne_Cricket_Ground "Melbourne Cricket Ground") despite having previously described it as "the most important moment of my life since I won a silver medal [there]".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-ISOR-5)

## Route

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Route")]

The Flame was lit during a ceremony in Olympia, as has been tradition at all the Summer Games since [those in 1936](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1936_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay "1936 Summer Olympics torch relay"). The Flame is initiated by using a parabolic mirror that concentrates the sun's rays. However, due to some cloud cover on the day of the ceremony, there was insufficient sunlight to create the required level of heat. A backup, lit on the previous day during rehearsals, was used instead. The remainder of the ceremony could then take place.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-OfficialReport-1)

The relay always begins in Greece and travels from Olympia to [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens") and the [Panathenaic Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panathenaic_Stadium "Panathenaic Stadium"). The [Hellenic Olympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellenic_Olympic_Committee "Hellenic Olympic Committee") arranged for the torch to be taken to several Greek islands, a first in the history of Olympic relays. The torch arrived in Athens on 20 May, after which it began a tour of Oceania. The Flame was flown firstly to [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam"), before moving to [Palau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palau "Palau"), [Micronesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micronesia "Micronesia"), [Nauru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nauru "Nauru"), the [Solomon Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon_Islands "Solomon Islands"), [Papua New Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papua_New_Guinea "Papua New Guinea"), [Vanuatu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vanuatu "Vanuatu"), [Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samoa "Samoa"), [American Samoa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Samoa "American Samoa"), the [Cook Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cook_Islands "Cook Islands"), [Tonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tonga "Tonga"), and [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand "New Zealand"). The relay had been scheduled to visit [Fiji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiji "Fiji"), but the country was omitted due to [ongoing government instability at that time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Fijian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "2000 Fijian coup d'état").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-OfficialReport-1)

After the island tour the Flame arrived in Australia on 8 June. The relay was an extensive journey around the country, involving 11,000 torch-bearers and a variety of modes of transport. On 27 June the Flame was taken underwater, a first in the history of torch relays. Marine biologist Wendy Craig Duncan carried a special version of the torch for a three-minute trip around [Agincourt Reef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agincourt_Reef?action=edit&redlink=1 "Agincourt Reef (page does not exist)"), a section of the [Great Barrier Reef](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Barrier_Reef "Great Barrier Reef") popular with divers. The torch was modified to carry a specially designed flare that would burn at 2,000 degrees Celsius underwater while remaining as aesthetically similar to the normal flame as possible.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-7) Shanthie De Mel, the first Sinhalese woman to carry the Olympic Flame, did the Torch run on day 33, July 30th on Ferntree Gully Road Mulgrave, Victoria, as Torch bearer 204.

The torch was brought off the plane by [Anna Booth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anna_Booth "Anna Booth") who chaired the 2000 Summer Olympics Torch Relay Committee. She met Governor-General, Sir [William Deane](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Deane "William Deane"), at Uluru and that began the torch's journey in Australia on 8 June. Booth later noted that this was the greatest honour of her life.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_Summer_Olympics_torch_relay#cite_note-8)
