The **Republic of the Congo**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-15) also known as the **Congo Republic**, **Congo-Brazzaville**, or simply the **Congo**,[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-16) is a country located on the western coast of [Central Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Africa "Central Africa") to the west of the [Congo River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River "Congo River"). It is bordered to the west by [Gabon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabon "Gabon"), to the northwest by [Cameroon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameroon "Cameroon"), to the northeast by the [Central African Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_African_Republic "Central African Republic"), to the southeast by the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), to the south by the [Angolan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angola "Angola")[exclave](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exclave "Exclave") of [Cabinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinda_Province "Cabinda Province"), and to the southwest by the Atlantic Ocean.

The region was dominated by [Bantu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_peoples "Bantu peoples")-speaking tribes at least 3,000 years ago, who built trade links leading into the Congo River basin. From the 13th century, the present-day territory was dominated by a confederation led by [Vungu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vungu "Vungu") which included [Kakongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakongo "Kakongo") and [Ngoyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngoyo "Ngoyo"). The [Tio Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tio_Kingdom "Tio Kingdom") emerged in the 14th century, and [Loango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Loango "Kingdom of Loango") in the 16th century. In the late 19th century France colonised the region and incorporated it into [French Equatorial Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Equatorial_Africa "French Equatorial Africa").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-CIAWFB-4) The Republic of the Congo was established on 28 November 1958 and gained independence from France in 1960. It was a [Marxist–Leninist state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxist%E2%80%93Leninist_state "Marxist–Leninist state") from 1969 to 1992, under the name [People's Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_the_Congo "People's Republic of the Congo") (PRC). After the introduction of multi-party elections in 1992, the democratically elected government was overthrown during the [civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo_Civil_War_(1997%E2%80%9399) "Republic of the Congo Civil War (1997–99)"), after which [Denis Sassou Nguesso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Sassou_Nguesso "Denis Sassou Nguesso"), who had previously served as president from 1979 to 1992, returned to office in 1997. He has remained president since then.

The Republic of the Congo is a member of the [African Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union "African Union"), the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"), [La Francophonie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_Francophonie "La Francophonie"), the [Economic Community of Central African States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_Community_of_Central_African_States "Economic Community of Central African States"), and the [Non-Aligned Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-Aligned_Movement "Non-Aligned Movement"). It is the fourth-largest [oil producer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oil_producer "Oil producer") in the [Gulf of Guinea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Guinea "Gulf of Guinea"), providing the country a degree of prosperity, with political and economic instability in some areas and unequal distribution of oil revenue nationwide. [Its economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Economy of the Republic of the Congo") is dependent on the oil sector[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-2018_nzaou_kongo-17) and economic growth slowed after [the post-2015 drop in oil prices](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010s_oil_glut "2010s oil glut").

[Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") is the most widely professed faith in the country. According to the 2024 rendition of the [World Happiness Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Happiness_Report "World Happiness Report"), the Republic of the Congo is ranked 89th among 140 nations.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-18)

## Etymology

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Republic_of_the_Congo&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Etymology")]

Further information: [Congo River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River "Congo River") and [Kongo people](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kongo_people "Kongo people")

It is named after the [Congo River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River "Congo River") whose name is derived from [Kongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kongo "Kingdom of Kongo"), a [Bantu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_peoples "Bantu peoples") kingdom that occupied its mouth around the time the [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal") first arrived in 1483[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-19) or 1484.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-20) The kingdom's name derived from its people, the [Bakongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakongo "Bakongo"), an [endonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endonym_and_exonym "Endonym and exonym") said to mean "hunters" ([Kongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kongo_language "Kongo language"): _mukongo_, _nkongo_).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-21)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-22)

During the period when France colonised it, it was known as the [French Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Congo "French Congo") or Middle Congo. The Republic of the Congo, or simply the Congo,[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-CIAWFB-4) is a distinct country from the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"), also known as the DR Congo.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-23)[Brazzaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazzaville "Brazzaville")'s name derives from the colony's founder, [Pierre Savorgnan de Brazzà](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_Savorgnan_de_Brazza "Pierre Savorgnan de Brazza"), an Italian nobleman whose title referred to the town of Brazzacco, in the [Italian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy")[comune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comune "Comune") of [Moruzzo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moruzzo "Moruzzo") in [Friuli-Venezia Giulia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friuli-Venezia_Giulia "Friuli-Venezia Giulia"), whose name derived from the [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_language "Latin language")_Brattius_ or _Braccius_, both meaning literally "[arm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arm "Arm")".[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-24)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Republic_of_the_Congo&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

Main article: [History of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "History of the Republic of the Congo")

[Bantu-speaking peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_peoples "Bantu peoples"), who founded tribes during the [Bantu expansions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_expansion "Bantu expansion"), mostly displaced and absorbed the earlier inhabitants of the region, the [Pygmy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Pygmies "African Pygmies") people, about 1500 BC. The [Bakongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bakongo "Bakongo"), a Bantu ethnic group that occupied parts of what later became Angola, Gabon, and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, formed the basis for ethnic affinities and rivalries among those countries.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1d/West_Central_Africa_1350CE.png/250px-West_Central_Africa_1350CE.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:West_Central_Africa_1350CE.png)

States of the western Congo Basin, c. 1350

By the 13th century, there were three main federations of states in the western Congo Basin. In the east were the [Seven Kingdoms of Kongo dia Nlaza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seven_Kingdoms_of_Kongo_dia_Nlaza "Seven Kingdoms of Kongo dia Nlaza"), considered to be the oldest and most powerful, which likely included [Nsundi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsundi "Nsundi"), [Mbata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mbata_Kingdom "Mbata Kingdom"), Mpangu, and possibly Kundi and Okanga. South of these was [Mpemba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpemba "Mpemba") which stretched from modern-day [Angola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angola "Angola") to the [Congo River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_River "Congo River"). It included various kingdoms such as [Mpemba Kasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mpemba_Kasi "Mpemba Kasi") and Vunda. To its west across the Congo River was a confederation of three small states; [Vungu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vungu "Vungu") (its leader), [Kakongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kakongo "Kakongo"), and [Ngoyo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngoyo "Ngoyo").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-25):24–25 Some Bantu kingdoms—including those of the [Kongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kongo_people "Kongo people"), the [Tio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tio_people "Tio people"), and [Loango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Loango "Kingdom of Loango")—built trade links leading into the [Congo Basin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo_Basin "Congo Basin").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dos2009-26) The [Tio Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tio_Kingdom "Tio Kingdom") formed in the 14th century;[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-Gongola-27) the association of kingship with [smithing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smithing "Smithing") is believed to have originated among the Tio before spreading to the kingdoms of Loango and [Kongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kongo "Kingdom of Kongo").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-Vansina_c16-28):439–42

The [Portuguese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Portugal "Kingdom of Portugal") explorer [Diogo Cão](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diogo_C%C3%A3o "Diogo Cão") reached the mouth of the Congo in 1484.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-DicImp-29) Commercial relationships grew between the inland Bantu kingdoms and European merchants who traded in commodities, manufactured goods, and people captured and enslaved in the [hinterlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hinterland "Hinterland"). After centuries as a central hub for transatlantic trade, direct European colonization of the Congo River delta began in the 19th century, subsequently eroding the power of the Bantu societies in the region.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-30)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Court_of_Loango.png/250px-Court_of_Loango.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Court_of_Loango.png)

The court of [N'Gangue M'voumbe Niambi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/N'Gangue_M'voumbe_Niambi "N'Gangue M'voumbe Niambi"), from the book _Description of Africa_ (1668)

The area north of the Congo River came under French sovereignty in 1880 as a result of [Pierre de Brazza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pierre_de_Brazza "Pierre de Brazza")'s treaty with Tio King [Iloo I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iloo_I "Iloo I").[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-32)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-DicImp-29) After the death of Iloo, his widow Queen [Ngalifourou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ngalifourou "Ngalifourou") upheld the terms of the treaty and became an ally to the colonizers.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-33) This Congo Colony became known first as [French Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Congo "French Congo"), then as Middle Congo in 1903.

In 1908, France organized [French Equatorial Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Equatorial_Africa "French Equatorial Africa") (AEF), comprising the Middle Congo, [Gabon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Gabon "French Gabon"), [Chad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Chad "French Chad"), and [Oubangui-Chari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oubangui-Chari "Oubangui-Chari") (which later became the [Central African Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_African_Republic "Central African Republic")). The French designated [Brazzaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazzaville "Brazzaville") as the federal capital. Economic development during the first 50 years of colonial rule in Congo centered on natural resource extraction. Construction of the [Congo–Ocean Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo%E2%80%93Ocean_Railway "Congo–Ocean Railway") following [World War I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I "World War I") has been estimated to have cost at least 14,000 lives.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-DicImp-29)

During the [Nazi occupation of France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_occupation_of_France "Nazi occupation of France") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), Brazzaville functioned as the symbolic capital of [Free France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_France "Free France") between 1940 and 1943.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-34) The [Brazzaville Conference of 1944](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazzaville_Conference_of_1944 "Brazzaville Conference of 1944") heralded a period of reform in French colonial policy. Congo "benefited" from the postwar expansion of colonial administrative and infrastructure spending as a result of its central geographic location within AEF and the federal capital at Brazzaville.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dos2009-26) It had a local legislature after the adoption of the 1946 constitution that established the [Fourth Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Fourth_Republic "French Fourth Republic").

Following the revision of the [French constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_France "Constitution of France") that established the [Fifth Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Fifth_Republic "French Fifth Republic") in 1958, AEF dissolved into its constituent parts, each of which became an autonomous colony within the [French Community](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Community "French Community"). During these reforms, Middle Congo became known as the Republic of the Congo in 1958[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dos2009-26) and published its first constitution in 1959.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-35) Antagonism between the [Mbochis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mbochi "Mbochi") (who favored [Jacques Opangault](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques_Opangault "Jacques Opangault")) and the [Laris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lari_people_(Congo) "Lari people (Congo)") and [Kongos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kongo_people "Kongo people") (who favored [Fulbert Youlou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulbert_Youlou "Fulbert Youlou"), the first black mayor elected in French Equatorial Africa) resulted in a series of riots in Brazzaville in February 1959, which the [French Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_Army "French Army") subdued.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-36)

Elections took place in April 1959. By the time the Congo became independent in August 1960, Opangault, the former opponent of Youlou, agreed to serve under him. Youlou, an avid anti-communist, became the first President of the Republic of the Congo.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-37) Since the political tension was so high in [Pointe-Noire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointe-Noire "Pointe-Noire"), Youlou moved the capital to Brazzaville.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

[![Image 17](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/2d/Alphonse_Massamba-Debat.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Alphonse_Massamba-Debat.png)

[Alphonse Massamba-Débat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Massamba-D%C3%A9bat "Alphonse Massamba-Débat")'s 1-party rule (1963–1968) attempted to implement a [political economic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_economy "Political economy") strategy of "[scientific socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_socialism "Scientific socialism")".

The Republic of the Congo became fully independent from France on 15 August 1960. Youlou ruled as the country's first president until labor elements and rival political parties instigated a [three-day uprising](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trois_Glorieuses_(1963) "Trois Glorieuses (1963)") that ousted him.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-38) The Congolese military took over the country and installed a civilian provisional government headed by [Alphonse Massamba-Débat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Massamba-D%C3%A9bat "Alphonse Massamba-Débat").

Under the 1963 constitution, Massamba-Débat was elected president for a five-year term.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dos2009-26) During [Massamba-Débat's term in office](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphonse_Massamba-D%C3%A9bat#Congo_under_Massamba-D%C3%A9bat_(1963%E2%80%931968) "Alphonse Massamba-Débat"), the regime adopted "[scientific socialism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_socialism "Scientific socialism")" as the country's constitutional ideology.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-shillington301-39) In 1964, Congo sent an official team with a single athlete at the [Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_Summer_Olympics "1964 Summer Olympics") for the first time in its history. In 1965, Congo established relations with the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union"), the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China"), [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea"), and [North Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vietnam "North Vietnam").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-shillington301-39) Under his presidency, the Congo began to [industrialize](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrialize "Industrialize"). Some large production units with large workforces were built: the textile factory of Kinsoundi, the palm groves of Etoumbi, the match factory of [Bétou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B%C3%A9tou "Bétou"), the shipyards of Yoro, etc. Health centers were created as well as school groups (colleges and elementary school). The country's school enrollment rate became the highest in Black Africa.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-40)

On the night of 14 to 15 February 1965, three public officials of the Republic of the Congo were kidnapped: [Lazare Matsocota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazare_Matsocota?action=edit&redlink=1 "Lazare Matsocota (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lazare%20Matsocota "fr:Lazare Matsocota")] (prosecutor of the Republic), [Joseph Pouabou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Pouabou?action=edit&redlink=1 "Joseph Pouabou (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph%20Pouabou "fr:Joseph Pouabou")] (President of the Supreme Court), and [Anselme Massouémé](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anselme_Massou%C3%A9m%C3%A9?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anselme Massouémé (page does not exist)")[[fr](https://fr.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anselme%20Massou%C3%A9m%C3%A9 "fr:Anselme Massouémé")] (director of the Congolese Information Agency). The bodies of two of these men were later found, mutilated, by the Congo River.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-41)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-42) Massamba-Débat's regime invited some hundred [Cuban](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuba "Cuba") army troops into the country to train his party's militia units. These troops helped his government survive a [_coup d'état_ in 1966](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1966_Republic_of_the_Congo_coup_d'%C3%A9tat_attempt "1966 Republic of the Congo coup d'état attempt") led by paratroopers loyal to future President [Marien Ngouabi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marien_Ngouabi "Marien Ngouabi"). Massamba-Débat's regime ended with a bloodless [_coup_ in September 1968](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1968_Republic_of_the_Congo_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1968 Republic of the Congo coup d'état").[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-shillington301-39)

Marien Ngouabi, who had participated in the coup, assumed the presidency on 31 December 1968. One year later, Ngouabi proclaimed the Congo Africa's first "people's republic", the [People's Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_the_Congo "People's Republic of the Congo"), and announced the decision of the National Revolutionary Movement to change its name to the [Congolese Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congolese_Party_of_Labour "Congolese Party of Labour") (PCT). He survived an [attempted _coup_ in 1972](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Republic_of_the_Congo_coup_d'%C3%A9tat_attempt "1972 Republic of the Congo coup d'état attempt") and was assassinated on 18 March 1977.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-43) An 11-member Military Committee of the Party (CMP) was then named to head an interim government, with [Joachim Yhombi-Opango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joachim_Yhombi-Opango "Joachim Yhombi-Opango") serving as president. Two years later, Yhombi-Opango was forced from power, and [Denis Sassou Nguesso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Sassou_Nguesso "Denis Sassou Nguesso") became the new president.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dos2009-26)

Sassou Nguesso aligned the country with the [Eastern Bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc") and signed a 20-year friendship pact with the Soviet Union. Over the years, Sassou had to rely more on [political repression](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_repression "Political repression") and less on [patronage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronage "Patronage") to maintain his dictatorship.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-shillington302-44) The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 resulted in the ending of Soviet aid to prop up the regime, and it abdicated power.

[Pascal Lissouba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pascal_Lissouba "Pascal Lissouba") who became Congo's first elected president (1992–1997) during the period of multi-party democracy attempted to implement economic reforms with IMF backing to liberalize the economy. In the years 1993 and 1994 the [first Republic of the Congo Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo_Civil_War_(1993%E2%80%931994) "Republic of the Congo Civil War (1993–1994)") occurred. In June 1996, IMF approved a three-year [SDR](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_drawing_rights "Special drawing rights") 69.5m (US$100m) [enhanced structural adjustment facility](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enhanced_structural_adjustment_facility "Enhanced structural adjustment facility") (ESAF) and was on the verge of announcing a renewed annual agreement when civil war broke out in Congo in 1997.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-45)

Congo's democratic progress was derailed in 1997 when Lissouba and Sassou started to fight for power in the [civil war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo_Civil_War_(1997%E2%80%931999) "Republic of the Congo Civil War (1997–1999)"). As presidential elections scheduled for July 1997 approached, tensions between the Lissouba and Sassou camps mounted. On 5 June, President Lissouba's government forces surrounded Sassou's compound in Brazzaville, and Sassou ordered members of his private militia (known as "Cobras") to resist. Thus began a four-month conflict that destroyed or damaged some of Brazzaville and caused tens of thousands of civilian deaths. In October, the Angolan government began an invasion of Congo to install Sassou in power and the Lissouba government fell. After that, Sassou declared himself president.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dos2009-26)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0a/Pro-constitutional_reform_demonstration_in_Brazzaville_-_2015-10_%2821518932913%29.jpg/250px-Pro-constitutional_reform_demonstration_in_Brazzaville_-_2015-10_%2821518932913%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Pro-constitutional_reform_demonstration_in_Brazzaville_-_2015-10_(21518932913).jpg)

A pro-constitutional reform rally in Brazzaville during October 2015. The constitution's reforms were subsequently approved in a disputed election that saw demonstrations and violence.

In the [elections in 2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo_presidential_election,_2002 "Republic of the Congo presidential election, 2002"), Sassou won with almost 90% of the vote cast. His two main rivals, Lissouba and Bernard Kolelas, were prevented from competing. A remaining rival, [André Milongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andr%C3%A9_Milongo "André Milongo") advised his supporters to boycott the elections and then withdrew from the race.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-freedomhouse-46) A [constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution "Constitution"), agreed upon by [referendum in January 2002](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo_constitutional_referendum,_2002 "Republic of the Congo constitutional referendum, 2002"), granted the president new powers, extended his term to seven years and introduced a new bicameral assembly. International observers took issue with the organization of the presidential election and the constitutional referendum, both of which were reminiscent in their organization of Congo's era of the 1-party state.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-47) Following the presidential elections, fighting restarted in the [Pool region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pool_Department "Pool Department") between government forces and rebels led by [Pastor Ntumi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pastor_Ntumi "Pastor Ntumi"); a peace treaty to end the conflict was signed in April 2003.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-48)

Sassou won the following [presidential election in July 2009](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo_presidential_election,_2009 "Republic of the Congo presidential election, 2009").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-49) According to the Congolese Observatory of Human Rights, a non-governmental organization, the election was marked by "very low" turnout and "fraud and irregularities".[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-50) In March 2015, Sassou announced that he wanted to run for yet another term in office and a [constitutional referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo_constitutional_referendum,_2015 "Republic of the Congo constitutional referendum, 2015") in October resulted in a [changed constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Constitution of the Republic of the Congo") that allowed him to run during the [2016 presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo_presidential_election,_2016 "Republic of the Congo presidential election, 2016"). He won the election believed by some to be fraudulent. After violent protests in the capital, Sassou attacked the Pool region where the [Ninja rebels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninja_(militia) "Ninja (militia)") of the civil war used to be based, in what was believed to be a distraction. This led to a revival of the Ninja rebels who launched attacks against the army in April 2016, leading 80,000 people to flee their homes. A ceasefire deal was signed in December 2017.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-51)

In 2023, the [Forest Massif of Odzala-Kokoua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odzala_National_Park "Odzala National Park") was listed as a natural [UNESCO World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO_World_Heritage_Site "UNESCO World Heritage Site").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-52)

## Geography

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Republic_of_the_Congo&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Geography")]

Main article: [Geography of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Geography of the Republic of the Congo")

Natural landscapes range from the [savanna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savanna "Savanna") plains in the North Niari flooded forests, to the Congo River, to the rugged mountains and forests of [Mayombe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mayombe "Mayombe"), and 170 km of beaches along the Atlantic coast.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-53)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e6/StatisticalData_1.svg/250px-StatisticalData_1.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:StatisticalData_1.svg)

Climate diagram for [Brazzaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazzaville "Brazzaville")

Congo is located in the central-western part of [sub-Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa"), along the [Equator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equator "Equator"), lying between latitudes [4°N](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4th_parallel_north "4th parallel north") and [5°S](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5th_parallel_south "5th parallel south"), and longitudes [11°](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/11th_meridian_east "11th meridian east") and [19°E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/19th_meridian_east "19th meridian east"). To the south and east of it is the [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"). It is bounded by [Gabon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gabon "Gabon") to the west, [Cameroon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cameroon "Cameroon") and the [Central African Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_African_Republic "Central African Republic") to the north, and [Cabinda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinda_(province) "Cabinda (province)") ([Angola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angola "Angola")) to the southwest. It has a coast on the Atlantic Ocean.

The southwest is a coastal plain for which the primary drainage is the [Kouilou-Niari River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kouilou-Niari_River "Kouilou-Niari River"); the interior of the country consists of a central plateau between 2 basins to the south and north. Forests are under increasing exploitation pressure.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-54) Congo had a 2018 [Forest Landscape Integrity Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forest_Landscape_Integrity_Index "Forest Landscape Integrity Index") mean score of 8.89/10, ranking it 12th globally out of 172 countries.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-FLII-Supplementary-55)

Congo lies within four terrestrial ecoregions: [Atlantic Equatorial coastal forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Equatorial_coastal_forests "Atlantic Equatorial coastal forests"), [Northwestern Congolian lowland forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_Congolian_lowland_forests "Northwestern Congolian lowland forests"), [Western Congolian swamp forests](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Congolian_swamp_forests "Western Congolian swamp forests"), and [Western Congolian forest–savanna mosaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Congolian_forest%E2%80%93savanna_mosaic "Western Congolian forest–savanna mosaic").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-DinersteinOlson2017-56) Since the country is located on the Equator, the climate is more consistent year-round, with the average day temperature a humid 24°C (75°F) and nights generally between 16°C (61°F) and 21°C (70°F). The average yearly rainfall ranges from 1,100 millimetres (43 in) in the [Niari Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niari_Valley "Niari Valley") in the south to over 2,000 millimetres (79 in) in central parts. The dry season is from June to August, while in the majority of the country, the wet season has 2 rainfall maxima: one in March–May and another in September–November.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-57)

In 2006–07, researchers from the [Wildlife Conservation Society](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wildlife_Conservation_Society "Wildlife Conservation Society") studied gorillas in "heavily forested" regions centered on the [Ouesso District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ouesso_District "Ouesso District") of the [Sangha Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangha_Region "Sangha Region"). They suggest a population on the order of 125,000 [western lowland gorillas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_lowland_gorilla "Western lowland gorilla") whose isolation from humans has been mostly preserved by "inhospitable" swamps.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-58)

## Government and politics

Main articles: [Politics of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Politics of the Republic of the Congo") and [Cabinet of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Cabinet of the Republic of the Congo")

See also: [Constitution of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Constitution of the Republic of the Congo"), [Foreign relations of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_relations_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Foreign relations of the Republic of the Congo"), [Armed Forces of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Armed Forces of the Republic of the Congo"), and [Biens mal acquis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biens_mal_acquis "Biens mal acquis")

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/3b/Vladimir_Putin_and_Denis_Sassou_Nguesso_%282025-05-09%29.jpg/250px-Vladimir_Putin_and_Denis_Sassou_Nguesso_%282025-05-09%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Vladimir_Putin_and_Denis_Sassou_Nguesso_(2025-05-09).jpg)

Congo's President [Denis Sassou Nguesso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Sassou_Nguesso "Denis Sassou Nguesso") with Russian President [Vladimir Putin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Putin "Vladimir Putin") in Moscow, Russia, on 9 May 2025

The government of the republic is a [semi-presidential system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semi-presidential_system "Semi-presidential system") with an elected president who appoints the [Council of Ministers, or Cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Cabinet of the Republic of the Congo"). The council, including the prime minister, is selected from the elected representatives in Parliament. Since the 1990s, the country has had a [multi-party political system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multi-party_system "Multi-party system") that is dominated by President [Denis Sassou Nguesso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Sassou_Nguesso "Denis Sassou Nguesso"). Sassou Nguesso is backed by his own [Congolese Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congolese_Labour_Party "Congolese Labour Party") ([French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_language "French language"): _Parti Congolais du Travail_) as well as a range of smaller parties.

Sassou's regime has seen [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_corruption "Political corruption") revelations, with attempts to censor them. One French investigation found over 110 bank accounts and dozens of "lavish properties" in France.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-59) Sassou denounced embezzlement investigations as "racist" and "colonial".[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-60)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-61)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-62) Denis Christel Sassou-Nguesso, son of Denis Sassou Nguesso, has been named in association with the [Panama Papers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_Papers "Panama Papers").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-63)

On 27 March 2015, Sassou Nguesso announced that his government would hold a referendum on changing the country's 2002 constitution to allow him to run for a third consecutive term in office.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-64) On 25 October, the government held a referendum on allowing Sassou Nguesso to run in the next election. The government claimed that the proposal was approved by 92% of voters, with 72% of eligible voters participating. The opposition who boycotted the referendum said that the government's statistics were false and the vote was a fake one.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-65) The election raised questions and was accompanied by civil unrest and police shootings of protesters;[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-66) at least 18 people were killed by security forces during opposition rallies leading up to the referendum held in October.

### Human rights

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Republic_of_the_Congo&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Human rights")]

Main article: [Human rights in the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Human rights in the Republic of the Congo")

See also: [LGBT rights in the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBT_rights_in_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "LGBT rights in the Republic of the Congo")

Some [Pygmies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pygmies "Pygmies") belong from birth to [Bantus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_peoples "Bantu peoples") in a relationship some refer to as slavery.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-globalpost-70)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-internationalreportingproject-71) The Congolese Human Rights Observatory says that the Pygmies are treated as property in the same way as pets.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-globalpost-70) On 30 December 2010, the [Congolese parliament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parliament_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Parliament of the Republic of the Congo") adopted a law to promote and protect the rights of indigenous peoples.[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] This law is "the first" of its kind in Africa.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-72)[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual\_of\_Style/Dates\_and\_numbers#Chronological\_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]

## Economy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Republic_of_the_Congo&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Economy")]

Main article: [Economy of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economy_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Economy of the Republic of the Congo")

See also: [Hydrocarbon exploration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hydrocarbon_exploration "Hydrocarbon exploration") and [List of companies of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_companies_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "List of companies of the Republic of the Congo")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/GDP_per_capita_development_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo.svg/250px-GDP_per_capita_development_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:GDP_per_capita_development_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo.svg)

GDP per capita development, 1950 to 2018

The economy is a mixture of village agriculture and handicrafts, an industrial sector based mainly on [petroleum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Petroleum "Petroleum"),[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-2018_nzaou_kongo-17)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-eia-73) support services, and a government characterized by budget problems and "overstaffing". Petroleum extraction has supplanted [forestry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forestry "Forestry") as the mainstay of the economy. In 2008, the oil sector accounted for 65% of the [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GDP "GDP"), 85% of government revenue, and 92% of exports.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-74) The country has untapped [mineral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mining_in_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Mining in the Republic of the Congo") wealth.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-2018_nzaou_kongo-17)

In the 1980s, rising oil revenues enabled the government to finance larger-scale development projects. GDP grew an average of 5% annually. The government has mortgaged a portion of its petroleum earnings, contributing to a "shortage of revenues". On 12 January 1994, the devaluation of [Franc Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CFA_franc "CFA franc") currencies by 50% resulted in an inflation of 46% in 1994, and inflation has subsided since.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-75)

Between 1994 and 1996, the economy underwent a difficult transition. The Congo took a number of measures to liberalize its economy, including reforming the tax, investment, labor, timber, and hydrocarbon codes. In 2002–03, Congo privatized banks, telecommunications, and transportation monopolies, to help improve an unreliable infrastructure. By the end of 1996 Congo had made progress in various areas targeted for reform. It made great strides toward macroeconomic stabilization through improving public finances and restructuring external debt. This change was accompanied by improvements in the structure of expenditures, with a reduction in personnel expenditures. Before June 1997, Congo and the United States ratified a bilateral investment treaty designed to facilitate and protect foreign investment. The country also adopted a new investment code intended to attract foreign capital. Despite these success, Congo's investment climate has challenges, offering few meaningful incentives for new investors.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-76)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/cf/Jeunes_filles_apprenant_la_couture_-_Ecole_Sp%C3%A9ciale_de_Brazzaville.jpg/250px-Jeunes_filles_apprenant_la_couture_-_Ecole_Sp%C3%A9ciale_de_Brazzaville.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jeunes_filles_apprenant_la_couture_-_Ecole_Sp%C3%A9ciale_de_Brazzaville.jpg)

Women learning to sew, Brazzaville

Economic reform efforts continued with the support of international organizations, including the [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank") and the [International Monetary Fund](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Monetary_Fund "International Monetary Fund"). The reform program came to a halt in June 1997 when civil war erupted. When Sassou Nguesso returned to power in October 1997, he publicly expressed interest in moving forward on [economic reforms](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_reform "Economic reform") and [privatization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization "Privatization") and in renewing cooperation with international financial institutions. Economic progress was "badly hurt" by slumping oil prices and the resumption of armed conflict in December 1998, which "worsened" the republic's budget deficit.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The administration presides over an "uneasy internal peace" and faces "difficult" economic problems of stimulating recovery and reducing poverty, with record-high oil prices since 2003. Natural gas and diamonds are other exports, while Congo was excluded from the [Kimberley Process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kimberley_Process "Kimberley Process") in 2004 amid allegations that most of its diamond exports were, in fact, being smuggled out of the neighboring [Democratic Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Democratic_Republic_of_the_Congo "Democratic Republic of the Congo"); it was re-admitted to the group in 2007.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-77)[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-78)

The Republic of the Congo has untapped base metal, gold, iron, and phosphate deposits.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-79) It is a member of the [Organization for the Harmonization of Business Law in Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_for_the_Harmonization_of_Business_Law_in_Africa "Organization for the Harmonization of Business Law in Africa") (OHADA).[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-ohada.com-80) The Congolese government signed an agreement in 2009 to lease 200,000 hectares of land to [South African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa "South Africa") farmers to reduce its dependence on imports.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-81)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-82) The GDP of the Republic of the Congo grew by 6% in 2014 and is expected to have grown by 7.5% in 2015.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-83)

In 2018, the Republic of the Congo joined the [Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organization_of_Petroleum_Exporting_Countries "Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries").[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-84)

[Congo–Ocean Railway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo%E2%80%93Ocean_Railway "Congo–Ocean Railway") was [built by forced laborers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congo%E2%80%93Ocean_Railway#History "Congo–Ocean Railway") during the 1930s. Some colonial architectural heritage is preserved. Restoration of architectural works is underway in Brazzaville, for example, at the Basilica of Sainte-Anne du Congo, which was completed in 2011.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-85)

## Demographics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Republic_of_the_Congo&action=edit&section=9 "Edit section: Demographics")]

Main article: [Demographics of the Republic of the Congo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_the_Republic_of_the_Congo "Demographics of the Republic of the Congo")

Population[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-UN_WPP-86)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-UN_WPP_2022-87)| Year | Million |
| --- | --- |
| 1950 | 0.8 |
| 2000 | 3.2 |

According to the official 2023 census, the population of the Congo numbers 6,142,180 people, up from 3,697,490 recorded by the 2007 census.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-88) Its population is concentrated in the southwestern portion, leaving the areas of tropical [jungle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jungle "Jungle") in the north virtually uninhabited. 70% of its total population lives in urban areas, namely in [Brazzaville](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazzaville "Brazzaville"), [Pointe-Noire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pointe-Noire "Pointe-Noire"), or one of the cities or villages lining the 534-kilometre (332 mi), railway which connects the two cities. In rural areas, industrial and commercial activity has declined in some years, leaving rural economies dependent on the government for support and subsistence.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dos2009-26)

Before the 1997 war, about 9,000 Europeans and other non-Africans lived in Congo, most of whom were [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/French_people "French people"); a fraction of this number remains.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dos2009-26) Around 300 [American](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") immigrants reside in the Congo.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dos2009-26)

The government 2025 [demographic and health survey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographic_and_Health_Surveys "Demographic and Health Surveys") (DHS) reported the [total fertility rate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Total_fertility_rate "Total fertility rate") had declined to 3.5 children born per woman, with a rate of 3.0 in urban areas and 5.3 in rural areas.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-dhs-3) The 2011–12 DHS found the TFR was 5.1 children born per woman, with 4.5 in urban areas and 6.5 in rural areas.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_the_Congo#cite_note-89)

**Ethiopia**,[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-16) officially the **Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia** (**FDRE**), is a [landlocked country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landlocked_country "Landlocked country") located in the [Horn of Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Horn_of_Africa "Horn of Africa") region of [East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa "East Africa"). It shares borders with [Eritrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrea "Eritrea") to the north, [Djibouti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Djibouti "Djibouti") to the northeast, [Somalia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia "Somalia") to the southeast, [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") to the south, [South Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Sudan "South Sudan") to the west, and [Sudan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan "Sudan") to the northwest. Ethiopia covers a land area of 1,104,300 km 2 (426,400 sq mi).[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-17)As of 2026[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Ethiopia&action=edit), it has around 138 million inhabitants, making it the [10th-most populous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population "List of countries and dependencies by population") country in the world and 2nd most populous country in Africa.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-:10-18) The national capital and largest city, [Addis Ababa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Addis_Ababa "Addis Ababa"), lies several kilometres west of the [East African Rift](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_Rift "East African Rift") that splits the country into the [African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Plate "African Plate") and [Somali](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_Plate "Somali Plate") tectonic plates.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-CIA2-19)

[Anatomically modern humans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_modern_human "Early modern human") emerged in what is now Ethiopia.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-20)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-22)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-23)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-24) In 980 BC, the Kingdom of [D'mt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%CA%BFmt "Dʿmt") extended its realm over Eritrea and the northern region of Ethiopia, while the [Kingdom of Aksum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum "Kingdom of Aksum") maintained a unified civilisation in the region for 900 years. Christianity arrived to the kingdom in 330 AD,[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-25) while Islam gained influence during the [first Hijra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_to_Abyssinia "Migration to Abyssinia") in 615.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-26) After the collapse of Aksum in 960, the [Zagwe dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zagwe_dynasty "Zagwe dynasty") ruled the north-central parts of Ethiopia. The [Shewan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shewa "Shewa") usurper, [Yekuno Amlak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yekuno_Amlak "Yekuno Amlak"), overthrew the dynasty in 1270 at the [Battle of Ansata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Ansata "Battle of Ansata"), inaugurating the [Ethiopian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Empire "Ethiopian Empire") and the Solomonic dynasty – asserting its lineage through Aksumite legitimacy by the biblical [Solomon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon "Solomon") and [Queen of Sheba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_of_Sheba "Queen of Sheba"), and [Menelik I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menelik_I "Menelik I") was the first emperor. Under Emperor [Amda Seyon I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amda_Seyon_I "Amda Seyon I") (r. 1314–1344), the empire grew in prestige through territorial expansion against neighbouring Muslim territories. Later, the [Ethiopian–Adal War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian%E2%80%93Adal_War "Ethiopian–Adal War") (1529–1543) weakened the empire and opened the way for the [Oromo expansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_expansions "Oromo expansions"). The growing influence of the Oromo at the Gondarine court ultimately contributed to the fragmentation known as [Zemene Mesafint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zemene_Mesafint "Zemene Mesafint"), beginning in 1769. [Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emperor_of_Ethiopia "Emperor of Ethiopia")[Tewodros II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tewodros_II "Tewodros II") ended the _Zemene Mesafint_ at the beginning of his reign in 1855, marking the reunification and modernisation of Ethiopia.

In the late 19th century, Ethiopia repelled foreign invasions from both [Egypt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egypt "Egypt") and [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy "Italy"), most notably defeating an Italian invasion at the [Battle of Adwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Adwa "Battle of Adwa") in 1896. Under Emperor [Menelik II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menelik_II "Menelik II"), it also [expanded its territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menelik_II's_conquests "Menelik II's conquests"), remaining independent during the [Scramble for Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scramble_for_Africa "Scramble for Africa") and establishing its current borders. Ethiopia lost its sovereignty in 1936, when [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy "Kingdom of Italy") under [Benito Mussolini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini "Benito Mussolini") invaded during the [Second Italo-Ethiopian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War "Second Italo-Ethiopian War"), and following Ethiopia's defeat, [Italian East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_East_Africa "Italian East Africa") was established. In 1941, during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), it was [liberated by the British Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_campaign_(World_War_II) "East African campaign (World War II)"), and its full sovereignty was [restored in 1944](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Ethiopian_Agreement#Negotiating_a_new_agreement "Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement"). The [Derg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derg "Derg"), a Soviet-backed military junta, took power in 1974 after [deposing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1974_Ethiopian_coup_d'%C3%A9tat "1974 Ethiopian coup d'état") Emperor [Haile Selassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Selassie "Haile Selassie") and the [Solomonic dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomonic_dynasty "Solomonic dynasty"), and ruled the country for nearly 17 years amidst the [Ethiopian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Civil_War "Ethiopian Civil War"). Following the [dissolution of the Derg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Derg "Fall of the Derg") in 1991, the [Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_People's_Revolutionary_Democratic_Front "Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front") (EPRDF) dominated the country with a [new constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1995_Constitution_of_Ethiopia "1995 Constitution of Ethiopia") and [ethnic-based federalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_federalism#Ethiopia "Ethnic federalism"). Since then, Ethiopia has suffered from prolonged and unsolved inter-ethnic clashes and political instability marked by [authoritarianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Authoritarianism "Authoritarianism"). From 2018, regional and ethnically based factions have carried out armed attacks in [multiple ongoing wars throughout Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_civil_conflict_(2018%E2%80%93present) "Ethiopian civil conflict (2018–present)").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-BBC1120-27)

Ethiopia is a [multi-ethnic state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multinational_state "Multinational state") with over 80 different [ethnic groups](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_ethnic_groups_in_Ethiopia "List of ethnic groups in Ethiopia"). [Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christianity "Christianity") is the most widely professed faith in the country, with the largest denomination being the [Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church "Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church"), followed by [Islam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_Ethiopia "Islam in Ethiopia") and a small percentage of [traditional faiths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traditional_African_religion "Traditional African religion"). The country is a founding member of the UN, and hosts the headquarters of the [African Union Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Union_Commission "African Union Commission") and many other global [non-governmental organisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-governmental_organisation "Non-governmental organisation") focused on Africa, also becoming a full member of [BRICS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BRICS "BRICS") in 2024.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-28) Ethiopia is one of the [least developed countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Least_developed_countries "Least developed countries") but is sometimes considered an [emerging power](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emerging_power "Emerging power"),[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-30) having the [fastest economic growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_African_countries_by_GDP_growth "List of African countries by GDP growth") in [sub-Saharan African](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa") countries because of [foreign direct investment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_direct_investment "Foreign direct investment") in expansion of agricultural and manufacturing industries; [agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture_in_Ethiopia "Agriculture in Ethiopia") is the country's largest economic sector, accounting for over 37% of the [GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") as of 2022. Although the Ethiopian economy has experienced consistent growth, in terms of [per capita income](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Per_capita_income "Per capita income") and the [Human Development Index](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_Human_Development_Index "List of countries by Human Development Index") the country remains among the poorest in Africa.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-31) Ethiopia faces numerous challenges, including high rates of [poverty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_in_Ethiopia "Poverty in Ethiopia"), [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_in_Ethiopia "Human rights in Ethiopia") violations, widespread ethnic discrimination, and a literacy rate of 60%.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-32)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-33)[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-:2-34)

## Names

See also: [Aethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aethiopia "Aethiopia")

Tradition holds that the name Ethiopia (ኢትዮጵያ) comes from the name of the first King of Ethiopia, Ethiop, or [Ethiopis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopis "Ethiopis").

Ayele Berkerie explains:

> According to an Ethiopian tradition, the term Ethiopia is derived from the word Ethiopis, a name of the Ethiopian king, the seventh in the ancestral lines. Metshafe Aksum or the Ethiopian Book of Aksum identifies Itiopis as the twelfth king of Ethiopia and the father of Aksumawi. The Ethiopians pronounce Ethiopia እትዮጵያ with a Sades or the sixth sound እ as in incorporate and the graph ጰ has no equivalent in English or Latin graphs. Ethiopis is believed to be the twelfth direct descendant of Adam. His father is identified as Kush, while his grandfather is known as Kam.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-35)

In the 15th-century Ge'ez _[Book of Axum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book\_of\_Axum "Book of Axum")_, the name is ascribed to a legendary individual called _Ityopp'is_. He was an extra-biblical son of [Cush, son of Ham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cush_(Bible) "Cush (Bible)"), said to have founded the city of [Axum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axum "Axum").[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Agrvt-36)

The [Greek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greek_language "Greek language") name Αἰθιοπία (from Αἰθίοψ, 'an Ethiopian') is a compound word, later explained as derived from the Greek words αἴθω and ὤψ (_eithō_ "I burn" + _ōps_ "face"). According to the [Liddell-Scott Jones Greek-English Lexicon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Greek%E2%80%93English_Lexicon "A Greek–English Lexicon"), the designation properly translates as _burnt-face_ in noun form and _red-brown_ in adjectival form.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-37) The historian [Herodotus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herodotus "Herodotus") used the appellation to denote those parts of Africa south of the [Sahara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahara "Sahara") that were then known within the [Ecumene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ecumene "Ecumene") (habitable world).[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Herodotus1-38) The earliest mention of the term is found in the works of [Homer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer "Homer"), where it is used to refer to two people groups, one in Africa and one in the east from eastern Turkey to India.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-39) This Greek name was borrowed into [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic "Amharic") as ኢትዮጵያ, _ʾĪtyōṗṗyā_.

In [Greco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Greece "Ancient Greece")-[Roman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") epigraphs, _Aethiopia_ was a specific toponym for ancient [Nubia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubia "Nubia").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Hatke-40) At least as early as c.850,[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-41) the name _Aethiopia_ also occurs in many translations of the [Hebrew Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_Bible "Hebrew Bible") (Tanakh) in allusion to Nubia. The ancient [Hebrew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_language "Hebrew language") texts identify Nubia instead as [Kush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Kush "Kingdom of Kush").[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-42) However, in the [Christian Bible](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bible#Christian_Bible "Bible"), the Greek term Aithiops does occur, referring to a servant of the [Kandake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kandake "Kandake"), the queen of Kush.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-43)

Following the Hellenic and biblical traditions, the [Monumentum Adulitanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monumentum_Adulitanum "Monumentum Adulitanum"), a 3rd-century inscription belonging to the Aksumite Empire, indicates that Aksum's ruler governed an area that was flanked to the west by the territory of Ethiopia and Sasu. The Aksumite King [Ezana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ezana_of_Axum "Ezana of Axum") eventually conquered Nubia the following century, and the Aksumites thereafter appropriated the designation "Ethiopians" for their own kingdom. In the [Ge'ez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ge%CA%BDez "Geʽez") version of the Ezana inscription, Aἰθίοπες is equated with the unvocalised _Ḥbšt_ and _Ḥbśt_ (Ḥabashat), and denotes for the first time the highland inhabitants of Aksum. This new [demonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demonym "Demonym") was subsequently rendered as _ḥbs_ ('Aḥbāsh) in [Sabaic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabaean_language "Sabaean language") and as _Ḥabasha_ in [Arabic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabic "Arabic").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Hatke-40) Derivatives of this are used in some languages that use loanwords from Arabic, for example in [Malay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malay_language "Malay language")_Habsyah_.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In English, and generally outside of Ethiopia, the country was historically known as [Abyssinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abyssinia "Abyssinia"). This toponym was derived from the Latinised form of the ancient _Habash_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-44)

## History

Main article: [History of Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Ethiopia "History of Ethiopia")

Further information: [Ethiopian historiography](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_historiography "Ethiopian historiography")

### Prehistory

![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1a/Ge%27ez.svg/40px-Ge%27ez.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)
