Main article: [Prehistoric Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistoric_Ethiopia "Prehistoric Ethiopia")

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9b/Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG/250px-Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Homo_Sapiens_Idaltu.JPG)

A _[Homo sapiens idaltu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herto\_Man "Herto Man")_ hominid skull

Several important finds have propelled Ethiopia and the surrounding region to the forefront of[palaeontology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleontology "Paleontology"). The oldest [hominid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hominidae "Hominidae") discovered to date in Ethiopia is the 4.2 million-year-old _[Ardipithecus ramidus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardipithecus "Ardipithecus")_ ([Ardi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ardi "Ardi")) found by [Tim D. White](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tim_D._White "Tim D. White") in 1994.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-OldestHuman-45) The most well-known hominid discovery is _[Australopithecus afarensis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australopithecus\_afarensis "Australopithecus afarensis")_ ([Lucy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_(hominid) "Lucy (hominid)")). Known locally as _Dinkinesh_, the specimen was found in the [Awash Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Awash_Valley "Awash Valley") of [Afar Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afar_Region "Afar Region") in 1974 by [Donald Johanson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Johanson "Donald Johanson"), and is one of the most complete and best-preserved adult [Australopithecine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australopithecus "Australopithecus") fossils ever uncovered. Lucy's taxonomic name refers to the region where the discovery was made. This hominid is estimated to have lived 3.2 million years ago.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Dinkinesh-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-iho1-48)

Ethiopia is also considered one of the earliest sites of the emergence of anatomically modern humans, _[Homo sapiens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human "Human")_. The oldest of these local fossil finds, the [Omo remains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omo_remains "Omo remains"), were excavated in the southwestern [Omo Kibish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Omo_Kibish_Formation "Omo Kibish Formation") area and have been dated to the [Middle Paleolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Paleolithic "Middle Paleolithic"), around 200,000 years ago.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Mcdougall2005-49) Additionally, skeletons of _[Homo sapiens idaltu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herto\_Man "Herto Man")_ were found at a site in the [Middle Awash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Awash "Middle Awash") valley. Dated to approximately 160,000 years ago, they may represent an extinct subspecies of _Homo sapiens_, or the immediate ancestors of anatomically modern humans.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-50) Archaic _Homo sapiens_ fossils excavated at the [Jebel Irhoud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jebel_Irhoud "Jebel Irhoud") site in Morocco have since been dated to an earlier period, about 300,000 years ago,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-51) while Omo-Kibish I (Omo I) from southern Ethiopia is the oldest anatomically modern _Homo sapiens_ skeleton currently known (196 ± 5 kya).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-52)

According to some anthropologists, the first [Afroasiatic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afroasiatic_languages "Afroasiatic languages")-speaking populations arrived in the region during the ensuing [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") era from the family's proposed [urheimat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afroasiatic_homeland "Afroasiatic homeland") ("original homeland") in the [Nile Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nile "Nile"),[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Zarins-53) or the [Near East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Near_East "Near East").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Aane-54) The majority of scholars today propose that the Afroasiatic family developed in northeast Africa because of the higher diversity of lineages in that region, a telltale sign of linguistic origin.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Blench143144-55)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-56)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-57)

In 2019, archaeologists discovered a 30,000-year-old [Middle Stone Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Stone_Age "Middle Stone Age") rock shelter at the [Fincha Habera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fincha_Habera,_Ethiopia "Fincha Habera, Ethiopia") site in [Bale Mountains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bale_Mountains "Bale Mountains") at an elevation of 3,469 m (11,381 ft) above sea level. At this high altitude, humans are susceptible both to [hypoxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypoxemia#Environmental_oxygen "Hypoxemia") and to extreme weather. According to a study published in the journal _[Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science\_(journal) "Science (journal)")_, this dwelling is proof of the earliest permanent human occupation at high altitude yet discovered. Thousands of animal bones, hundreds of stone tools, and ancient fireplaces were discovered, revealing a diet that featured giant [mole rats](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spalacidae "Spalacidae").[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-59)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-61)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-63)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-64)

Evidence of some of the earliest known stone-tipped projectile weapons (a characteristic tool of _Homo sapiens_), the stone tips of [javelins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Javelin "Javelin") or throwing spears, were discovered in 2013 at the Ethiopian site of [Gademotta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gademotta "Gademotta"), which date to around 279,000 years ago.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-SahlePLOS1-65) In 2019, additional Middle Stone Age projectile weapons were found at Aduma, dated 100,000–80,000 years ago, in the form of points considered likely to belong to darts delivered by spear throwers.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Sahle-66)

### Antiquity

Main articles: [Dʿmt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%CA%BFmt "Dʿmt") and [Kingdom of Aksum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum "Kingdom of Aksum")

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg/250px-KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:KingEndybisEthiopia227-235CE.jpg)

[Aksumite currency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksumite_currency "Aksumite currency") of the [Aksumite king](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axumite_kings "Axumite kings")[Endybis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endybis "Endybis") (227–235), [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum")[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-67)

In 980 BC, Dʿmt was established in present-day Eritrea and the northern part of Ethiopia in the [Tigray Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigray_Region "Tigray Region"), and is widely believed to be the successor state to [Punt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_of_Punt "Land of Punt"). This polity's capital was located at [Yeha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yeha "Yeha") in what is now northern Ethiopia. Most modern historians consider this civilisation to be a native Ethiopian one, although in earlier times many suggested it was [Sabaean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sabaeans "Sabaeans")-influenced because of the latter's hegemony of the [Red Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Sea "Red Sea").[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Munro-Hay57-68)

Other scholars regard Dʿmt as the result of a union of Afroasiatic-speaking cultures of the Cushitic and Semitic branches; namely, local [Agaw peoples](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agaw_people "Agaw people") and Sabaeans from Southern Arabia. However, Ge'ez, the ancient Semitic language of Ethiopia, is thought to have developed independently from the Sabaean language. As early as 2000 BC, other Semitic speakers were living in Ethiopia and Eritrea where Ge'ez developed.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-69)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-70) Sabaean influence is now thought to have been minor, limited to a few localities, and disappearing after a few decades or a century. It may have been a trading or military colony in alliance with the Ethiopian civilisation of Dʿmt or some other proto-[Axumite](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axumite "Axumite") state.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Munro-Hay57-68)

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png/250px-The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Kingdom_of_Aksum.png)

The [Empire of Axum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Aksum "Kingdom of Aksum") at its peak in the 6th century

After the fall of Dʿmt during the 4th century BC, the Ethiopian plateau came to be dominated by smaller successor kingdoms. In the 1st century AD, the Kingdom of Aksum emerged in what is now Tigray Region and Eritrea. According to the medieval _Book of Axum_, the kingdom's first capital, Mazaber, was built by Itiyopis, son of Cush.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Agrvt-36) Aksum would later at times extend its rule into Yemen on the other side of the Red Sea.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-71) The Persian prophet [Mani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mani_(prophet) "Mani (prophet)") listed Axum with Rome, Persia, and China as one of the four great powers of his era, during the 3rd century.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-72) It is also believed that there was a connection between Egyptian and Ethiopian churches. There is faint evidence that the Aksumites were associated with the Queen of Sheba, via their royal inscription.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-:5-73)

Around 316 AD, [Frumentius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frumentius "Frumentius") and his brother Edesius from [Tyre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tyre,_Lebanon "Tyre, Lebanon") accompanied their uncle on a voyage to Ethiopia. When the vessel stopped at a Red Sea port, the natives killed all the travellers except the two brothers, who were taken to the court as [slaves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_Ethiopia "Slavery in Ethiopia"). They were given positions of trust by the monarch, and they converted members of the royal court to Christianity. Frumentius became the first bishop of Aksum.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-isbn0-313-32273-2-74) A coin dated to 324 shows that Ethiopia was the second country to officially adopt Christianity (after Armenia did so in 301), although the religion may have been at first confined to court circles; it was the first major power to do so. The Aksumites were accustomed to the Greco-Roman sphere of influence, but they embarked on significant cultural ties and trade connections between the [Indian subcontinent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent "Indian subcontinent") and the Roman Empire via the [Silk Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road"), primarily exporting [ivory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivory_trade "Ivory trade"), tortoise shell, gold and emeralds, and importing silk and spices.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-:5-73)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-britishmuseum.org-75) The country's gold production in 2015 is 9 tonnes.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-76)

### Middle Ages

Main article: [Ethiopia in the Middle Ages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia_in_the_Middle_Ages "Ethiopia in the Middle Ages")

The kingdom adopted the name "Ethiopia" during the reign of Ezana in the 4th century. After the conquest of Kingdom of Kush in 330, the Aksumite territory reached its peak between the 5th and 6th centuries.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Munro-Hay57-68) This period was interrupted by several incursions into the South Arabian protectorate, including [Jewish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jews "Jews")[Dhu Nuwas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dhu_Nuwas "Dhu Nuwas") of the [Himyarite Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himyarite_Kingdom "Himyarite Kingdom") and the [Aksumite–Persian wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aksumite%E2%80%93Persian_wars "Aksumite–Persian wars"). In 575, the Aksumites [besieged and retook Sana'a](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sasanian_reconquest_of_Yemen "Sasanian reconquest of Yemen") following the assassination of its governor [Sayf ibn Dhī Yazan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sayf_ibn_Dhi_Yazan "Sayf ibn Dhi Yazan"). The Red Sea was left to the [Rashidun Caliphate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rashidun_Caliphate "Rashidun Caliphate") in 646, and the port city of [Adulis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adulis "Adulis") was plundered by Arab Muslims in the 8th century; along with irrevocable [land degradation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_degradation "Land degradation"), claimed [climate change](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Climate_change_(general_concept) "Climate change (general concept)") and sporadic rainfall precipitation from 730 to 760,[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-77) these factors likely caused the kingdom to decline in power as part of an important trade route.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Munro-Hay57-68)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-:12-78) Aksum came to an end in 960 when [Queen Gudit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gudit "Gudit") defeated the last king of Aksum.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-79) In response, the remnant of the Aksumite population shifted into the southern region and establish the Zagwe dynasty, changing its capital to [Lalibela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lalibela "Lalibela").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-80) Zagwe's rule ended when [Amhara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amhara_people "Amhara people") nobleman Yekuno Amlak revolted against King [Yetbarak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yetbarak "Yetbarak") and established the Ethiopian Empire (known by the [exonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exonym "Exonym") "Abyssinia").

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/da/Bete_Medhane_Alem_in_Lalibela.JPG/250px-Bete_Medhane_Alem_in_Lalibela.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Bete_Medhane_Alem_in_Lalibela.JPG)

[Biete Medhane Alem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biete_Medhane_Alem "Biete Medhane Alem"), built during [Zagwe dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zagwe_dynasty "Zagwe dynasty") in the Middle Ages

The Ethiopian Empire initiated territorial expansion under the leadership of Amda Seyon I. He launched campaigns against his Muslim adversaries to the east, resulting in a significant shift in the balance of power in favour of the Christians for the next two centuries. After Amda Seyon's successful eastern campaigns, most of the Muslim principalities in the Horn of Africa came under the suzerainty of the Ethiopian Empire. Stretching from [Gojjam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gojjam "Gojjam") to the Somali Coast in [Zeila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeila "Zeila").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-81) Among these Muslim entities was the [Sultanate of Ifat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sultanate_of_Ifat "Sultanate of Ifat"). During the reign of Emperor [Zara Yaqob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zara_Yaqob "Zara Yaqob"), the Ethiopian Empire reached its pinnacle. His rule was marked by the consolidation of territorial acquisitions from earlier rulers, the oversight of the construction of numerous churches and monasteries, the active promotion of literature and art, and the strengthening of central imperial authority.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-82)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-:3b-83)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-FOOTNOTEConnelKillion2011160-84) Ifat's successor, the [Adal Sultanate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adal_Sultanate "Adal Sultanate"),[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-85) tried to conquer Ethiopia during the Ethiopian–Adal War, but was ultimately defeated at the 1543 [Battle of Wayna Daga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Wayna_Daga "Battle of Wayna Daga").[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-86)

By the 16th century, an influx of migration by ethnic [Oromo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_people "Oromo people") into northern parts of the region fragmented the empire's power. Embarking from present-day [Guji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guji_Zone "Guji Zone") and [Borena Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borena_Zone "Borena Zone"), the Oromos were largely motivated by several folkloric conceptions—beginning with _Moggaasaa_[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-87) and _Liqimssa_—many of whom related to their raids. This persisted until _gada_ of Meslé.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-FOOTNOTEPankhurst1997301-88)[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-:8-89) According to [Abba Bahrey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bahrey "Bahrey"), the earliest expansion occurred under Emperor [Dawit II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dawit_II "Dawit II") ([_luba_ Melbah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luba_Melbah "Luba Melbah")), when they encroached to [Bale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bale_Province,_Ethiopia "Bale Province, Ethiopia") before invading Adal Sultanate.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Reference-90)

During the 16th and 17th centuries, Ethiopia saw major diplomatic contact with [Portugal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portugal "Portugal"), which was primarily religious in nature. Beginning in 1555,[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-91) Portuguese Jesuits attempted to develop Roman Catholicism as the state religion. After several failures, they sent several missionaries in 1603, including the most influential, Spanish Jesuit [Pedro Paez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pedro_P%C3%A1ez "Pedro Páez").[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-92) Under Emperor [Susenyos I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susenyos_I "Susenyos I"), Roman Catholicism became the state religion of the Ethiopian Empire in 1622.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Parfitt2019-93) This decision caused an uprising by the Orthodox populace.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-berndl2005-94)

### Early Modern Period (1632–1855)

Main articles: [Gondarine period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondarine_period "Gondarine period") and [Zemene Mesafint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zemene_Mesafint "Zemene Mesafint")

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f4/Paris%2C_Biblioth%C3%A8que_nationale_de_France%2C_Ethiopien_d%27Abbadie_215%2C_folio_1r.JPEG/250px-Paris%2C_Biblioth%C3%A8que_nationale_de_France%2C_Ethiopien_d%27Abbadie_215%2C_folio_1r.JPEG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Paris,_Biblioth%C3%A8que_nationale_de_France,_Ethiopien_d'Abbadie_215,_folio_1r.JPEG)

A copy of 17th century philosophical and [ethical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethical "Ethical") treatise by [Ethiopian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian "Ethiopian") philosopher [Zara Yaqob](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zara_Yaqob "Zara Yaqob")

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_%2823869587160%29.jpg/250px-Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_%2823869587160%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Fasil_Ghebbi_IV_(23869587160).jpg)

[Fasil Ghebbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fasil_Ghebbi "Fasil Ghebbi"), one of the key castles of the [Gondarine period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondarine_period "Gondarine period")

In 1632, Emperor [Fasilides](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fasilides "Fasilides") halted Roman Catholic state administration, restoring [Orthodox Tewahedo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthodox_Tewahedo "Orthodox Tewahedo") as the state religion.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Parfitt2019-93) Fasilides' reign solidified imperial power, relocating the capital to [Gondar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondar "Gondar") in 1636, marking the beginning of the "[Gondarine period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gondarine_period "Gondarine period")".[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-95) He reclaimed lands, and exiled [Jesuits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesuits "Jesuits") to [Fremona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fremona "Fremona"). During his rule, Fasilides constructed the iconic royal fortress, [Fasil Ghebbi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fasil_Ghebbi "Fasil Ghebbi"), built forty-four churches,[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-96) and revived [Ethiopian art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_art "Ethiopian art"). He is also credited with building seven stone bridges over the [Blue Nile River](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blue_Nile_River "Blue Nile River").[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-97)

Gondar's power declined after the death of [Iyasu I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iyasu_I "Iyasu I") in 1706. Following [Iyasu II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iyasu_II "Iyasu II")'s death in 1755, Empress [Mentewab](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mentewab "Mentewab") brought her brother, [Ras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_(title) "Ras (title)") Wolde Leul, to Gondar, making him Ras Bitwaded. This led to regnal conflict between Mentewab's _Quaregnoch_ and the Wollo group led by Wubit. In 1767, Ras [Mikael Sehul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mikael_Sehul "Mikael Sehul"), a regent in [Tigray Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tigray_Province "Tigray Province"), seized Gondar, killing the child [Iyoas I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iyoas_I "Iyoas I") in 1769, the reigning emperor, and installed 70-year-old [Yohannes II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yohannes_II "Yohannes II").[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-98)

Between 1769 and 1855, Ethiopia witnessed the Zemene Mesafint or "Age of Princes," a period of isolation. Emperors became figureheads, controlled by regional lords and noblemen like _Ras_ Mikael Sehul, Ras [Wolde Selassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolde_Selassie "Wolde Selassie") of Tigray, and by the [Yejju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yejju "Yejju") Oromo dynasty of the [Wara Sheh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zemene_Mesafint#Wara_Sheh_rulers_(Yejju)_(1784%E2%80%931855) "Zemene Mesafint"), including Ras [Gugsa of Yejju](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gugsa_of_Yejju "Gugsa of Yejju"). Before the Zemene Mesafint, Emperor Iyoas I had introduced the Oromo language (_Afaan Oromo_) at court, replacing Amharic.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-99)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-100)

### Age of Imperialism (1855–1916)

Main articles: [British expedition to Abyssinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_expedition_to_Abyssinia "British expedition to Abyssinia"), [Menelik's Invasions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menelik's_Invasions "Menelik's Invasions"), [Egyptian–Ethiopian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian%E2%80%93Ethiopian_War "Egyptian–Ethiopian War"), [First Italo-Ethiopian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Italo-Ethiopian_War "First Italo-Ethiopian War"), and [Mahdist War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahdist_War "Mahdist War")

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f4/T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg/250px-T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:T%C3%A9wodros_II_-_2.jpg)

Emperor Tewodros II (r. 1855–1868) brought an end to Zemene Mesafint.

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2d/Menelik_-_Adoua-2_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Menelik_-_Adoua-2_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Menelik_-_Adoua-2_(cropped).jpg)

Emperor [Menelik II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menelik_II "Menelik II") defended Ethiopia's sovereignty during the age of imperialism.

Ethiopian isolationism ended following a British mission that concluded with an alliance between the two nations, but it was not until 1855 that the Amhara kingdoms of northern Ethiopia (Gondar, Gojjam, and Shewa) were briefly united after the power of the emperor was restored beginning with the reign of Tewodros II.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-Middleton2015-101)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-102) Tewodros II began a process of consolidation, centralisation, and state-building that would be continued by succeeding emperors. This process reduced the power of regional rulers, restructured the empire's administration, and created a professional army. These changes created the basis for establishing the effective sovereignty and territorial integrity of the Ethiopian state.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-103) In 1875 and 1876, Ottoman and Egyptian forces, accompanied by many European and American advisors, twice [invaded Abyssinia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptian%E2%80%93Ethiopian_War "Egyptian–Ethiopian War") but were initially defeated.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-104) From 1885 to 1889 (under [Yohannes IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yohannes_IV "Yohannes IV")), Ethiopia joined the [Mahdist War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahdist_War "Mahdist War") allied to [Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom_of_Great_Britain_and_Ireland "United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland"), the Ottomans, and Egypt against the Sudanese Mahdist State. In 1887, Menelik II, king of Shewa, invaded the [Emirate of Harar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emirate_of_Harar "Emirate of Harar") after his victory at the [Battle of Chelenqo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chelenqo "Battle of Chelenqo").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-105) On 10 March 1889, Yohannes IV was killed by the Sudanese Khalifah Abdullah's army whilst leading his army in the [Battle of Gallabat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gallabat "Battle of Gallabat").[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-106)

Ethiopia, in roughly its current form, began under the reign of Menelik II, who was Emperor from 1889 until his death in 1913. From his base in the central province of Shewa, Menelik set out to annex territories to the south, east, and west[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-ReferenceA-107)—areas inhabited by the Oromo, [Sidama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sidama_people "Sidama people"), Gurage, [Welayta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welayta_people "Welayta people"), and other peoples.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-igg-108) He achieved this with the help of _Ras_[Gobana Dacche](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gobana_Dacche "Gobana Dacche")'s Shewan Oromo militia, which occupied lands that had not been held since [Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_ibn_Ibrahim_al-Ghazi "Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi")'s war, as well as other areas that had never been under Ethiopian rule.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-109)

For his leadership, despite opposition from more traditional elements of society, Menelik II was heralded as a national hero. He had signed the [Treaty of Wuchale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Wuchale "Treaty of Wuchale") with Italy in May 1889, by which Italy would recognise Ethiopia's sovereignty so long as Italy could control an area north of Ethiopia (now part of modern Eritrea). In return, Italy was to provide Menelik with weapons and support him as emperor. The Italians used the time between the signing of the treaty and its ratification by the Italian government to expand their territorial claims. This [First Italo-Ethiopian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Italo-Ethiopian_War "First Italo-Ethiopian War") culminated in the Battle of Adwa on 1 March 1896, in which Italy's colonial forces were defeated by the Ethiopians.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-igg-108)[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-110) During this time, about a third of the population died in the [Great Ethiopian Famine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Famines_in_Ethiopia "Famines in Ethiopia") (1888 to 1892),[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-111)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-112) and the [rinderpest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1890s_African_rinderpest_epizootic "1890s African rinderpest epizootic") swept through the area, destroying much of the herd economy.

### Haile Selassie I era (1916–1974) and Italian colonial rule (1936-1941)

Main articles: [Second Italo-Ethiopian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Italo-Ethiopian_War "Second Italo-Ethiopian War"), [Italian Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Ethiopia "Italian Ethiopia"), [Italian East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_East_Africa "Italian East Africa"), [Federation of Ethiopia and Eritrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Ethiopia_and_Eritrea "Federation of Ethiopia and Eritrea"), and [Eritrean War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrean_War_of_Independence "Eritrean War of Independence")

[![Image 26](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Ethiopian_Soldiers_Korean_War.jpg/250px-Ethiopian_Soldiers_Korean_War.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ethiopian_Soldiers_Korean_War.jpg)

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d1/Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg/250px-Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Emperor_Haile_Selassie_I_with_President_FDR.jpg)

[Emperor Haile Selassie I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Selassie "Haile Selassie") with U.S. president [Franklin D. Roosevelt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_D._Roosevelt "Franklin D. Roosevelt") during the end of World War II[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_]

The early 20th century was marked by the reign of Emperor Haile Selassie (_Ras Tafari_). He came to power after [Lij Iyasu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lij_Iyasu "Lij Iyasu") was deposed, and undertook [a nationwide modernisation campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernisation_under_Haile_Selassie "Modernisation under Haile Selassie") from 1916 when he was made a _Ras_ and Regent (_[Inderase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inderase "Inderase")_) for the [Empress Regnant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Queen_regnant "Queen regnant")[Zewditu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zewditu "Zewditu"), and became the _de facto_ ruler of the Ethiopian Empire. Following Zewditu's death on 2 November 1930, he succeeded her as emperor.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-113) In 1931, Haile Selassie endowed Ethiopia with [its first constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1931_Constitution_of_Ethiopia "1931 Constitution of Ethiopia") in emulation of Imperial Japan's [1890 Constitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meiji_Constitution "Meiji Constitution").[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-114)

The independence of Ethiopia was interrupted by the Second Italo-Ethiopian War, beginning when it was invaded by [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy#Fascist_regime_(1922%E2%80%931943) "Kingdom of Italy") in early October 1935, and by subsequent Italian rule of the country (1936–1941) after Italian victory in the war.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-115) Italy, however, never managed to secure the country in its totality, due to resistance from the [Arbegnoch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arbegnoch "Arbegnoch"); this made Ethiopia, along with [Liberia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberia "Liberia"), the only African country to never be fully colonised.[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-116)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-117) Following the entry of Italy into World War II, [British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Empire "British Empire") forces, together with the Arbegnoch, liberated Ethiopia in the course of the East African campaign in 1941. The country was placed under [British military administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occupied_Enemy_Territory_Administration_(Ethiopia) "Occupied Enemy Territory Administration (Ethiopia)"), and then Ethiopia's full [sovereignty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereignty "Sovereignty") was restored with the signing of the [Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Ethiopian_Agreement "Anglo-Ethiopian Agreement") in December 1944.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-118)

On 24 October 1945, Ethiopia became a founding member of the [United Nations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations"). In 1952, Haile Selassie orchestrated a [federation with Eritrea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federation_of_Ethiopia_and_Eritrea "Federation of Ethiopia and Eritrea"). He dissolved it in 1962 and annexed Eritrea, resulting in the [Eritrean War of Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrean_War_of_Independence "Eritrean War of Independence").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-119) Haile Selassie also played a leading role in the formation of the [Organisation of African Unity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Organisation_of_African_Unity "Organisation of African Unity") (OAU).[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-120) Opinion within Ethiopia turned against Haile Selassie, owing to the worldwide [1973 oil crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis") causing a sharp increase in gasoline prices starting on 13 February 1974, leading to student and worker protests.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-121) The feudal oligarchical cabinet of [Aklilu Habte-Wold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aklilu_Habte-Wold "Aklilu Habte-Wold") was toppled, and a new government was formed with [Endelkachew Makonnen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Endelkachew_Makonnen "Endelkachew Makonnen") serving as Prime Minister.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-122)

### Derg era (1974–1991)

See also: [Ethiopian Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Revolution "Ethiopian Revolution"), [Derg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derg "Derg"), [People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Democratic_Republic_of_Ethiopia "People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia"), [Ethiopian Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Civil_War "Ethiopian Civil War"), [Red Terror](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Terror_(Ethiopia) "Red Terror (Ethiopia)"), and [1983–1985 famine in Ethiopia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1983%E2%80%931985_famine_in_Ethiopia "1983–1985 famine in Ethiopia")

[![Image 28](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/c7/Mengistu_Haile_Mariam_3.jpg/250px-Mengistu_Haile_Mariam_3.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mengistu_Haile_Mariam_3.jpg)

[Mengistu Haile Mariam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mengistu_Haile_Mariam "Mengistu Haile Mariam") was sentenced to death [_in absentia_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_in_absentia "Trial in absentia") for committing [crimes during his rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Terror_(Ethiopia) "Red Terror (Ethiopia)").

Haile Selassie's rule ended on 12 September 1974, when he was deposed by the Derg, a committee made up of military and police officers.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-123) After the execution of [60 former government and military officials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massacre_of_the_Sixty "Massacre of the Sixty"),[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-124) the new [Provisional Military Administrative Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provisional_Military_Administrative_Council "Provisional Military Administrative Council") abolished the monarchy in March 1975 and established Ethiopia as a [Marxist-Leninist state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxist-Leninist_state "Marxist-Leninist state").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-125) The abolition of [feudalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudalism "Feudalism"), increased [literacy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literacy "Literacy"), [nationalisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationalisation "Nationalisation"), and sweeping [land reform](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reform "Land reform") including the [resettlement and villagisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Resettlement_and_villagisation_in_Ethiopia "Resettlement and villagisation in Ethiopia") from the [Ethiopian Highlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Highlands "Ethiopian Highlands") became priorities.[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia#cite_note-126)
